    Qh,i,jn​(t)Q_{h,i,j}^{n}(t): number of class-ii tasks waiting for human review on the judge path; Zi,jn​(t)Z_{i,j}^{n}(t): number of class-ii tasks in human service on the judge path.

Capacity constraints impose

∑iXin​(t)\displaystyle\sum_{i}X_{i}^{n}(t) ≤nwn,∑iYin(t)≤njn,∑i(Zi,dn(t)+Zi,jn(t))≤nhn,∀t≥0.\displaystyle\leq n_{w}^{n},\qquad\sum_{i}Y_{i}^{n}(t)\leq n_{j}^{n},\qquad\sum_{i}\big(Z_{i,d}^{n}(t)+Z_{i,j}^{n}(t)\big)\leq n_{h}^{n},\qquad\forall t\geq 0. (6)

Control (routing and scheduling).

Control actions determine (i) admissions from queues into service in each resource pool, and (ii) routing of AI-Worker outputs from the routing buffer to either the judge path or the direct human path. We encode these decisions through cumulative control processes:

  • •

    Uw,in​(t)U_{w,i}^{n}(t): number of class-ii tasks admitted into AI-Worker service by time tt.

  • •

    Uj,in​(t)U_{j,i}^{n}(t): number of class-ii tasks admitted into judge service by time tt.

  • •

    Uh,i,dn​(t)U_{h,i,d}^{n}(t) and Uh,i,jn​(t)U_{h,i,j}^{n}(t): numbers of class-ii tasks admitted into human service on the direct and judge paths by time tt.

Routing of AI-Worker completions is encoded by controlled counting processes Sw→j,in​(t)S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t) and Sw→h,in​(t)S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t), which count (respectively) the numbers of class-ii worker completions routed to the judge and routed directly to humans by time tt. These routing processes can only increase at AI-Worker completion epochs and must satisfy

Sw→j,in​(t)+Sw→h,in​(t)=Sw,in​(t),∀t≥0,S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t)+S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t)=S_{w,i}^{n}(t),\qquad\forall t\geq 0, (7)

where Sw,in​(t)S_{w,i}^{n}(t) is the total number of class-ii AI-Worker service completions by time tt (defined below via a random time-change). Scheduling decisions specify how the available server capacity in each pool is allocated across classes, and are reflected in the evolution of the admission processes above.

Flow counting processes and balance equations.

To formalize the dynamics, we define cumulative flow processes. Let Ain​(t)A_{i}^{n}(t) be the cumulative number of exogenous class-ii arrivals by time tt. Let Bw,in​(t)B_{w,i}^{n}(t) be the cumulative number of abandonments from the worker queue.

Service completions are split by routing/outcomes:

  • •

    Total AI-Worker completions: Sw,in​(t)S_{w,i}^{n}(t); routing splits: Sw→j,in​(t)S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t) and Sw→h,in​(t)S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t) satisfying (7).

  • •

    Judge completions that are rejected (rework) and accepted (sent to humans): Sj→w,in​(t)S_{j\to w,i}^{n}(t) and Sj→h,in​(t)S_{j\to h,i}^{n}(t).

  • •

    Human completions on the direct path that fail and succeed: Sh,d→w,in​(t)S_{h,d\to w,i}^{n}(t) and Sh,d→c,in​(t)S_{h,d\to c,i}^{n}(t).

  • •

    Human completions on the judge path that fail and succeed: Sh,j→w,in​(t)S_{h,j\to w,i}^{n}(t) and Sh,j→c,in​(t)S_{h,j\to c,i}^{n}(t).

Define the cumulative number of successfully completed class-ii tasks as

Cin​(t):=Sh,d→c,in​(t)+Sh,j→c,in​(t).C_{i}^{n}(t):=S_{h,d\to c,i}^{n}(t)+S_{h,j\to c,i}^{n}(t). (8)

Under the exponential assumptions, these flows admit standard random time-change representations. Let {NA,i,NB,i,Nw,i,Nj→w,i,Nj→h,i,Nh,d→w,i,Nh,d→c,i,Nh,j→w,i,Nh,j→c,i}i∈ℐ\{N_{A,i},N_{B,i},N_{w,i},N_{j\to w,i},N_{j\to h,i},N_{h,d\to w,i},N_{h,d\to c,i},N_{h,j\to w,i},N_{h,j\to c,i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} be mutually independent unit-rate Poisson processes. Then for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} and t≥0t\geq 0:

Ain​(t)\displaystyle A_{i}^{n}(t) =NA,i​(λin​t),\displaystyle=N_{A,i}\!\big(\lambda_{i}^{n}\,t\big), (9)
Bw,in​(t)\displaystyle B_{w,i}^{n}(t) =NB,i​(∫0tθi​Qw,in​(s)​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{B,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\theta_{i}\,Q_{w,i}^{n}(s)\,ds\right), (10)
Sw,in​(t)\displaystyle S_{w,i}^{n}(t) =Nw,i​(∫0tμw,i​Xin​(s)​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{w,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}\,X_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds\right), (11)
Sj→w,in​(t)\displaystyle S_{j\to w,i}^{n}(t) =Nj→w,i​(∫0tμj,i​Yin​(s)​prej,i​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{j\to w,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{j,i}\,Y_{i}^{n}(s)\,p_{\mathrm{rej},i}\,ds\right), (12)
Sj→h,in​(t)\displaystyle S_{j\to h,i}^{n}(t) =Nj→h,i​(∫0tμj,i​Yin​(s)​ppass,i​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{j\to h,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{j,i}\,Y_{i}^{n}(s)\,p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\,ds\right), (13)

where Sj→w,inS_{j\to w,i}^{n} and Sj→h,inS_{j\to h,i}^{n} are independent thinnings of the total judge completion process Sj,in​(t):=Nj,i​(∫0tμj,i​Yin​(s)​𝑑s)S_{j,i}^{n}(t):=N_{j,i}(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{j,i}Y_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds), satisfying Sj→w,in​(t)+Sj→h,in​(t)=Sj,in​(t)S_{j\to w,i}^{n}(t)+S_{j\to h,i}^{n}(t)=S_{j,i}^{n}(t) almost surely. Analogous representations hold for the human completion splits given below. The worker-routing counts Sw→j,in​(t)S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t) and Sw→h,in​(t)S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t) are policy-controlled splitting processes constrained by (7); in particular, they are integer-valued, nondecreasing, and can only jump when Sw,in​(t)S_{w,i}^{n}(t) jumps. In particular, for the direct human path, incorrect outputs occur with probability αi\alpha_{i}, so

Sh,d→w,in​(t)=Nh,d→w,i​(∫0tμh,i​Zi,dn​(s)​αi​𝑑s),Sh,d→c,in​(t)=Nh,d→c,i​(∫0tμh,i​Zi,dn​(s)​(1−αi)​𝑑s).S_{h,d\to w,i}^{n}(t)=N_{h,d\to w,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,Z_{i,d}^{n}(s)\,\alpha_{i}\,ds\right),\qquad S_{h,d\to c,i}^{n}(t)=N_{h,d\to c,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,Z_{i,d}^{n}(s)\,(1-\alpha_{i})\,ds\right). (14)

For the judge path, conditional on judge acceptance, the probability that an output is incorrect equals (1−qacc,i)(1-q_{\mathrm{acc},i}), hence

Sh,j→w,in​(t)\displaystyle S_{h,j\to w,i}^{n}(t) =Nh,j→w,i​(∫0tμh,i​Zi,jn​(s)​(1−qacc,i)​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{h,j\to w,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,Z_{i,j}^{n}(s)\,(1-q_{\mathrm{acc},i})\,ds\right), (15)
Sh,j→c,in​(t)\displaystyle S_{h,j\to c,i}^{n}(t) =Nh,j→c,i​(∫0tμh,i​Zi,jn​(s)​qacc,i​𝑑s).\displaystyle=N_{h,j\to c,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,Z_{i,j}^{n}(s)\,q_{\mathrm{acc},i}\,ds\right). (16)

The state and flow processes satisfy the following balance equations for each class ii and all t≥0t\geq 0:

Qw,in​(t)\displaystyle Q_{w,i}^{n}(t) =Qw,in​(0)+Ain​(t)+Sj→w,in​(t)+Sh,d→w,in​(t)+Sh,j→w,in​(t)−Uw,in​(t)−Bw,in​(t),\displaystyle=Q_{w,i}^{n}(0)+A_{i}^{n}(t)+S_{j\to w,i}^{n}(t)+S_{h,d\to w,i}^{n}(t)+S_{h,j\to w,i}^{n}(t)-U_{w,i}^{n}(t)-B_{w,i}^{n}(t), (17)
Xin​(t)\displaystyle X_{i}^{n}(t) =Xin​(0)+Uw,in​(t)−(Sw→j,in​(t)+Sw→h,in​(t)),\displaystyle=X_{i}^{n}(0)+U_{w,i}^{n}(t)-\big(S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t)+S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t)\big), (18)
Qj,in​(t)\displaystyle Q_{j,i}^{n}(t) =Qj,in​(0)+Sw→j,in​(t)−Uj,in​(t),\displaystyle=Q_{j,i}^{n}(0)+S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t)-U_{j,i}^{n}(t), (19)
Yin​(t)\displaystyle Y_{i}^{n}(t) =Yin​(0)+Uj,in​(t)−(Sj→w,in​(t)+Sj→h,in​(t)),\displaystyle=Y_{i}^{n}(0)+U_{j,i}^{n}(t)-\big(S_{j\to w,i}^{n}(t)+S_{j\to h,i}^{n}(t)\big), (20)
Qh,i,dn​(t)\displaystyle Q_{h,i,d}^{n}(t) =Qh,i,dn​(0)+Sw→h,in​(t)−Uh,i,dn​(t),\displaystyle=Q_{h,i,d}^{n}(0)+S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t)-U_{h,i,d}^{n}(t), (21)
Zi,dn​(t)\displaystyle Z_{i,d}^{n}(t) =Zi,dn​(0)+Uh,i,dn​(t)−(Sh,d→w,in​(t)+Sh,d→c,in​(t)),\displaystyle=Z_{i,d}^{n}(0)+U_{h,i,d}^{n}(t)-\big(S_{h,d\to w,i}^{n}(t)+S_{h,d\to c,i}^{n}(t)\big), (22)
Qh,i,jn​(t)\displaystyle Q_{h,i,j}^{n}(t) =Qh,i,jn​(0)+Sj→h,in​(t)−Uh,i,jn​(t),\displaystyle=Q_{h,i,j}^{n}(0)+S_{j\to h,i}^{n}(t)-U_{h,i,j}^{n}(t), (23)
Zi,jn​(t)\displaystyle Z_{i,j}^{n}(t) =Zi,jn​(0)+Uh,i,jn​(t)−(Sh,j→w,in​(t)+Sh,j→c,in​(t)),\displaystyle=Z_{i,j}^{n}(0)+U_{h,i,j}^{n}(t)-\big(S_{h,j\to w,i}^{n}(t)+S_{h,j\to c,i}^{n}(t)\big), (24)

where the cumulative admission processes Uw,in​(t),Uj,in​(t),Uh,i,dn​(t),Uh,i,jn​(t)U_{w,i}^{n}(t),U_{j,i}^{n}(t),U_{h,i,d}^{n}(t),U_{h,i,j}^{n}(t) are policy-controlled and must respect the capacity constraints.

Admissible policies.

Following standard queueing-control conventions, we define a policy 𝝅n\bm{\pi}^{n} as the collection of all non-primitive processes in the nnth system: state processes (queues and in-service counts), cumulative flow processes (arrivals, abandonments, service completions, routing splits, and successful completions), and control processes (admissions and routing decisions), each indexed by class i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}. All control processes are adapted to the natural filtration generated by the primitive processes (arrivals, service completions, abandonments) and past control actions. Let Πn\Pi^{n} denote the set of policies satisfying:

  • (i)

    The resulting processes satisfy the capacity constraints and balance equations (17)–(24) for all t≥0t\geq 0.

  • (ii)

    The policy is event-driven: each control process U⋅,in​(t)U_{\cdot,i}^{n}(t) and each routing process Sw→j,in​(t),Sw→h,in​(t)S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t),S_{w\to h,i}^{n}(t) can change only at arrival epochs, abandonment epochs, service-completion epochs, or at t=0t=0.

  • (iii)

    Service is non-preemptive and within each class queues are served in first-come-first-served order.

In Section 3 we replace these stochastic dynamics by a steady-state fluid approximation that yields a tractable optimization problem.

Objective.

With reward weights ri>0r_{i}>0, we consider the long-run average throughput objective

max𝝅n∈Πnlim infT→∞1n​T​𝔼𝝅n​[∑i∈ℐri​Cin​(T)],\max_{\bm{\pi}^{n}\in\Pi^{n}}\quad\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\bm{\pi}^{n}}\Big[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}\,C_{i}^{n}(T)\Big], (25)

over the admissible policy class Πn\Pi^{n}. The remainder of the paper focuses on structural insights obtainable from the associated steady-state fluid model.

3 Fluid Model

The stochastic network in Section 2.3 is analytically intractable due to the high-dimensional state space and the feedback loops created by rework. We adopt a many-server fluid approximation that is justified by a fluid limit as the system scales. For any process Wn​(t)W^{n}(t) in system nn, define its fluid-scaled version W¯n​(t):=Wn​(t)/n\bar{W}^{n}(t):=W^{n}(t)/n and let n→∞n\to\infty. In the limit, stochastic fluctuations average out and the network is described by deterministic flow-balance equations and capacity constraints.

Fluid model.

We write

(qw,i​(t),xi​(t),qj,i​(t),yi​(t),qh,i,d​(t),zi,d​(t),qh,i,j​(t),zi,j​(t))\big(q_{w,i}(t),x_{i}(t),q_{j,i}(t),y_{i}(t),q_{h,i,d}(t),z_{i,d}(t),q_{h,i,j}(t),z_{i,j}(t)\big)

for generic deterministic fluid trajectories that arise as subsequential limits of the fluid-scaled stochastic processes. These functions satisfy, for all t≥0t\geq 0 and all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, the flow-balance equations

qw,i​(t)\displaystyle q_{w,i}(t) =qw,i​(0)+ai​(t)+sj→w,i​(t)+sh,d→w,i​(t)+sh,j→w,i​(t)−uw,i​(t)−bw,i​(t),\displaystyle=q_{w,i}(0)+a_{i}(t)+s_{j\to w,i}(t)+s_{h,d\to w,i}(t)+s_{h,j\to w,i}(t)-u_{w,i}(t)-b_{w,i}(t), (26)
xi​(t)\displaystyle x_{i}(t) =xi​(0)+uw,i​(t)−sw→j,i​(t)−sw→h,i​(t),\displaystyle=x_{i}(0)+u_{w,i}(t)-s_{w\to j,i}(t)-s_{w\to h,i}(t),
qj,i​(t)\displaystyle q_{j,i}(t) =qj,i​(0)+sw→j,i​(t)−uj,i​(t),\displaystyle=q_{j,i}(0)+s_{w\to j,i}(t)-u_{j,i}(t),
yi​(t)\displaystyle y_{i}(t) =yi​(0)+uj,i​(t)−sj→w,i​(t)−sj→h,i​(t),\displaystyle=y_{i}(0)+u_{j,i}(t)-s_{j\to w,i}(t)-s_{j\to h,i}(t),
qh,i,d​(t)\displaystyle q_{h,i,d}(t) =qh,i,d​(0)+sw→h,i​(t)−uh,i,d​(t),\displaystyle=q_{h,i,d}(0)+s_{w\to h,i}(t)-u_{h,i,d}(t),
zi,d​(t)\displaystyle z_{i,d}(t) =zi,d​(0)+uh,i,d​(t)−sh,d→w,i​(t)−sh,d→c,i​(t),\displaystyle=z_{i,d}(0)+u_{h,i,d}(t)-s_{h,d\to w,i}(t)-s_{h,d\to c,i}(t),
qh,i,j​(t)\displaystyle q_{h,i,j}(t) =qh,i,j​(0)+sj→h,i​(t)−uh,i,j​(t),\displaystyle=q_{h,i,j}(0)+s_{j\to h,i}(t)-u_{h,i,j}(t),
zi,j​(t)\displaystyle z_{i,j}(t) =zi,j​(0)+uh,i,j​(t)−sh,j→w,i​(t)−sh,j→c,i​(t).\displaystyle=z_{i,j}(0)+u_{h,i,j}(t)-s_{h,j\to w,i}(t)-s_{h,j\to c,i}(t).

Here u⋅,i​(t)u_{\cdot,i}(t) are cumulative admissions into service (policy controls), bw,i​(t)b_{w,i}(t) is cumulative abandonment from the work queue, and s⋅→⋅,i(t)s_{\cdot\to\cdot,i}(t) are cumulative routing/service-completion flows between nodes.

Mean-rate primitives.

Let vi​(t)v_{i}(t) denote the judge-routed worker service level: the instantaneous in-service mass of class ii at workers whose completions are routed to the judge, satisfying 0≤vi​(t)≤xi​(t)0\leq v_{i}(t)\leq x_{i}(t). The primitive arrivals, abandonments, and service-driven routing flows evolve at their mean rates:

ai​(t)\displaystyle a_{i}(t) =λi​t,bw,i​(t)=∫0tθi​qw,i​(s)​𝑑s,\displaystyle=\lambda_{i}\,t,\qquad b_{w,i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\theta_{i}\,q_{w,i}(s)\,ds,
sw→j,i​(t)\displaystyle s_{w\to j,i}(t) =∫0tμw,i​vi​(s)​𝑑s,sw→h,i​(t)=∫0tμw,i​(xi​(s)−vi​(s))​𝑑s,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}\,v_{i}(s)\,ds,\qquad s_{w\to h,i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}\,\big(x_{i}(s)-v_{i}(s)\big)\,ds,
sj→w,i​(t)\displaystyle s_{j\to w,i}(t) =∫0tμj,i​yi​(s)​prej,i​𝑑s,sj→h,i​(t)=∫0tμj,i​yi​(s)​ppass,i​𝑑s,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{j,i}\,y_{i}(s)\,p_{\mathrm{rej},i}\,ds,\qquad s_{j\to h,i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{j,i}\,y_{i}(s)\,p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\,ds,
sh,d→w,i​(t)\displaystyle s_{h,d\to w,i}(t) =∫0tμh,i​zi,d​(s)​αi​𝑑s,sh,d→c,i​(t)=∫0tμh,i​zi,d​(s)​(1−αi)​𝑑s,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,d}(s)\,\alpha_{i}\,ds,\qquad s_{h,d\to c,i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,d}(s)\,(1-\alpha_{i})\,ds,
sh,j→w,i​(t)\displaystyle s_{h,j\to w,i}(t) =∫0tμh,i​zi,j​(s)​(1−qacc,i)​𝑑s,sh,j→c,i​(t)=∫0tμh,i​zi,j​(s)​qacc,i​𝑑s.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,j}(s)\,(1-q_{\mathrm{acc},i})\,ds,\qquad s_{h,j\to c,i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,j}(s)\,q_{\mathrm{acc},i}\,ds. (27)

Equivalently, vi​(t)=ϕi​(t)​xi​(t)v_{i}(t)=\phi_{i}(t)\,x_{i}(t) for some ϕi​(t)∈[0,1]\phi_{i}(t)\in[0,1].

Capacity constraints.

Let x⁡(t):=∑ixi​(t)x(t):=\sum_{i}x_{i}(t), y⁡(t):=∑iyi​(t)y(t):=\sum_{i}y_{i}(t), and z⁡(t):=∑i(zi,d​(t)+zi,j​(t))z(t):=\sum_{i}\big(z_{i,d}(t)+z_{i,j}(t)\big). The fluid model enforces the normalized capacity constraints

0≤x⁡(t)≤nw,0≤y⁡(t)≤nj,0≤z⁡(t)≤nh,∀t≥0.0\leq x(t)\leq n_{w},\qquad 0\leq y(t)\leq n_{j},\qquad 0\leq z(t)\leq n_{h},\qquad\forall t\geq 0. (28)
{assumption}

[Convergence of initial state] The fluid-scaled initial states converge in probability to a deterministic limit: for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I},

1n​(Qw,in​(0),Xin​(0),Qj,in​(0),Yin​(0),Qh,i,dn​(0),Zi,dn​(0),Qh,i,jn​(0),Zi,jn​(0))→𝑃𝐳0,i,\frac{1}{n}\bigl(Q_{w,i}^{n}(0),\,X_{i}^{n}(0),\,Q_{j,i}^{n}(0),\,Y_{i}^{n}(0),\,Q_{h,i,d}^{n}(0),\,Z_{i,d}^{n}(0),\,Q_{h,i,j}^{n}(0),\,Z_{i,j}^{n}(0)\bigr)\xrightarrow{P}\mathbf{z}_{0,i},

where 𝐳0,i\mathbf{z}_{0,i} is a deterministic vector.

Theorem 3.1 (Fluid limit)

Fix any finite horizon T>0T>0. Under Assumption 3 and any admissible policy sequence {𝛑n}n≥1\{\bm{\pi}^{n}\}_{n\geq 1} with 𝛑n∈Πn\bm{\pi}^{n}\in\Pi^{n} for each nn, the sequence of fluid-scaled processes is tight in 𝔻⁡([0,T],ℝd)\mathbb{D}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d}) under the Skorokhod J1J_{1} topology, where dd is the total dimension of the process vector. Moreover, any subsequential weak limit is almost surely continuous and satisfies the fluid model equations (26)–(27) and the capacity constraints (28) on [0,T][0,T], with initial state given by Assumption 3.

Steady-state fluid optimization.

We now focus on steady-state operating points of the fluid model above. Fix the exogenous parameters (λi,θi,μw,i,μj,i,μh,i,nw,nj,nh)(\lambda_{i},\theta_{i},\mu_{w,i},\mu_{j,i},\mu_{h,i},n_{w},n_{j},n_{h}) and the quality parameters summarized by ppass,ip_{\mathrm{pass},i}, prej,ip_{\mathrm{rej},i}, and qacc,iq_{\mathrm{acc},i} in (1)–(3). Let qw,iq_{w,i} be the steady-state work-queue mass, and let (xi,yi,zi,d,zi,j)(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i,d},z_{i,j}) be the steady-state in-service masses at workers, judges, humans (direct), and humans (judge path), respectively. Introduce an auxiliary variable viv_{i} representing the judge-routed worker service level, satisfying 0≤vi≤xi0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i} (equivalently, vi=ϕi​xiv_{i}=\phi_{i}x_{i} for some ϕi∈[0,1]\phi_{i}\in[0,1]). The steady-state completion rate of class ii equals λi−θi​qw,i\lambda_{i}-\theta_{i}q_{w,i} since abandonment occurs only at the work queue. We therefore solve:

max{qw,i,xi,yi,zi,d,zi,j,vi}\displaystyle\max_{\{q_{w,i},\,x_{i},\,y_{i},\,z_{i,d},\,z_{i,j},\,v_{i}\}}\quad ∑i=1Iri​(λi−θi​qw,i)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}r_{i}\,(\lambda_{i}-\theta_{i}q_{w,i}) (29a)
s.t. μw,i​vi=μj,i​yi,∀i∈ℐ,\displaystyle\mu_{w,i}\,v_{i}\;=\;\mu_{j,i}\,y_{i},\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}, (29b)
μw,i​(xi−vi)=μh,i​zi,d,∀i∈ℐ,\displaystyle\mu_{w,i}\,(x_{i}-v_{i})\;=\;\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,d},\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}, (29c)
μj,i​yi​ppass,i=μh,i​zi,j,∀i∈ℐ,\displaystyle\mu_{j,i}\,y_{i}\,p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\;=\;\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,j},\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}, (29d)
λi+μj,i​yi​prej,i+μh,i​zi,d​αi+μh,i​zi,j​(1−qacc,i)\displaystyle\lambda_{i}+\mu_{j,i}\,y_{i}\,p_{\mathrm{rej},i}+\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,d}\,\alpha_{i}+\mu_{h,i}\,z_{i,j}\,(1-q_{\mathrm{acc},i})
=μw,i​xi+θi​qw,i,∀i∈ℐ,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\;=\;\mu_{w,i}\,x_{i}+\theta_{i}\,q_{w,i},\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}, (29e)
∑i=1Ixi≤nw,∑i=1Iyi≤nj,∑i=1I(zi,d+zi,j)≤nh,\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}x_{i}\leq n_{w},\quad\sum_{i=1}^{I}y_{i}\leq n_{j},\quad\sum_{i=1}^{I}(z_{i,d}+z_{i,j})\leq n_{h}, (29f)
0≤vi≤xi,qw,i,xi,yi,zi,d,zi,j≥0,∀i∈ℐ.\displaystyle 0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i},\quad q_{w,i},x_{i},y_{i},z_{i,d},z_{i,j}\geq 0,\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}. (29g)

The optimization (29) is the steady-state specialization of the fluid model. The objective (29a) maximizes weighted throughput: λi−θi​qw,i\lambda_{i}-\theta_{i}q_{w,i} is the completion rate of class ii, since tasks abandon only from the work queue at rate θi​qw,i\theta_{i}q_{w,i}. Constraints (29b)–(29d) are flow-balance equations linking adjacent nodes. Constraint (29b) balances worker-to-judge flow: the rate at which workers complete tasks routed to judges (μw,i​vi\mu_{w,i}v_{i}) must equal the rate at which judges process them (μj,i​yi\mu_{j,i}y_{i}). Constraint (29c) balances the direct path: the rate of worker completions sent directly to humans (μw,i​(xi−vi)\mu_{w,i}(x_{i}-v_{i})) equals the human processing rate on the direct path (μh,i​zi,d\mu_{h,i}z_{i,d}). Constraint (29d) balances the judge-to-human flow: the rate at which judges pass tasks (μj,i​yi​ppass,i\mu_{j,i}y_{i}p_{\mathrm{pass},i}) equals the human processing rate on the judge path (μh,i​zi,j\mu_{h,i}z_{i,j}). Constraint (29e) is the work-queue balance. The inflow comprises fresh arrivals λi\lambda_{i}, judge rejections μj,i​yi​prej,i\mu_{j,i}y_{i}p_{\mathrm{rej},i}, human failures on the direct path μh,i​zi,d​αi\mu_{h,i}z_{i,d}\alpha_{i}, and human failures on the judge path μh,i​zi,j​(1−qacc,i)\mu_{h,i}z_{i,j}(1-q_{\mathrm{acc},i}). The outflow is worker service μw,i​xi\mu_{w,i}x_{i} plus abandonment θi​qw,i\theta_{i}q_{w,i}. Constraint (29f) enforces resource capacities: aggregate in-service mass at workers, judges, and humans cannot exceed nwn_{w}, njn_{j}, and nhn_{h}, respectively.

Reduced multi-class LP.

Eliminating the intermediate variables (yi,zi,d,zi,j,qw,i)(y_{i},z_{i,d},z_{i,j},q_{w,i}) via flow balance yields an equivalent LP in only (xi,vi)(x_{i},v_{i}). Using yi=(μw,i/μj,i)​viy_{i}=(\mu_{w,i}/\mu_{j,i})\,v_{i}, zi,d=(μw,i/μh,i)​(xi−vi)z_{i,d}=(\mu_{w,i}/\mu_{h,i})(x_{i}-v_{i}), and zi,j=(μw,i/μh,i)​ppass,i​viz_{i,j}=(\mu_{w,i}/\mu_{h,i})\,p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\,v_{i}, the human capacity constraint becomes ∑i(μw,i/μh,i)​(xi−prej,i​vi)≤nh\sum_{i}(\mu_{w,i}/\mu_{h,i})(x_{i}-p_{\mathrm{rej},i}\,v_{i})\leq n_{h}, where prej,i=1−ppass,ip_{\mathrm{rej},i}=1-p_{\mathrm{pass},i}. The objective simplifies via the identity ppass,i​qacc,i=(1−αi)​(1−βi(I))p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\,q_{\mathrm{acc},i}=(1-\alpha_{i})(1-\beta_{i}^{(I)}) to ∑iri​μw,i​(1−αi)​(xi−βi(I)​vi)\sum_{i}r_{i}\,\mu_{w,i}(1-\alpha_{i})(x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}\,v_{i}). The reduced LP is:

max(xi,vi)i∈ℐ\displaystyle\max_{(x_{i},v_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{I}}}\quad ∑i∈ℐri​μw,i​(1−αi)​(xi−βi(I)​vi)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}\,\mu_{w,i}(1-\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}\big) (30a)
s.t. 0≤vi≤xi,xi−βi(I)​vi≤λiμw,i​(1−αi),i∈ℐ,\displaystyle 0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i},\quad x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}\leq\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{w,i}(1-\alpha_{i})},\qquad i\in\mathcal{I}, (30b)
∑i∈ℐxi≤nw,∑i∈ℐμw,iμj,i​vi≤nj,\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x_{i}\leq n_{w},\quad\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}\,v_{i}\leq n_{j}, (30c)
∑i∈ℐμw,iμh,i​(xi−prej,i​vi)≤nh.\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{h,i}}\big(x_{i}-p_{\mathrm{rej},i}v_{i}\big)\leq n_{h}. (30d)

Given an optimal solution, a corresponding judge-flow proportion can be recovered by ϕi∗=vi∗/xi∗\phi_{i}^{*}=v_{i}^{*}/x_{i}^{*} when xi∗>0x_{i}^{*}>0 (and ϕi∗:=0\phi_{i}^{*}:=0 when xi∗=0x_{i}^{*}=0).

4 Phase Transitions and Priority Reversal in Optimal Judge Allocation

The general formulation in Section 3 yields a tractable linear program, but the structural properties of the optimal allocation are not apparent from the LP alone. This section reveals that optimal judge allocation exhibits sharp phase transitions, that is, discrete structural changes at computable capacity thresholds where the system bottleneck shifts between resource types. We analyze two canonical cases. The single-class case (Section 4.1) establishes how to use the judge: a four-phase structure governs judge intensity and reveals a regime in which the system should reduce judge usage even when judge capacity is available, because rework crowds out new production. The two-class case (Section 4.2) establishes who gets the judge: optimal priority can reverse across bottleneck regimes, with a complementarity zone where both classes share judge capacity.

4.1 Single-Class System: The Four-Phase Structure

We begin with the single-class case (I=1I=1), which reveals the fundamental trade-off governing judge allocation.

The quality-quantity trade-off.

The judge serves as a quality filter: it screens worker outputs and rejects those it deems incorrect, reducing the burden on human reviewers. However, this filtering carries a cost. Type I errors (false rejections) send correct outputs back to workers for unnecessary rework, consuming worker capacity. When workers are abundant, this rework cost is negligible, and the system benefits from maximizing judge usage. When workers are scarce, rework competes with new production for limited capacity, and the system must balance filtering benefits against efficiency losses.

The optimal judge allocation ϕ∗\phi^{*} depends on which resource is the bottleneck. As human capacity varies from scarce to abundant, the bottleneck shifts, and the optimal allocation exhibits phase transitions: discrete changes at specific capacity thresholds.

Specializing the reduced multi-class LP (30) to I=1I=1 yields a 2D LP; we state it in Appendix 9.3. To isolate the impact of resource scarcity, we assume an overloaded regime.

{assumption}

[Overloaded regime] Throughout this section, we assume the system is overloaded: λμw​(1−α)≥nw\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{\mu_{w}(1-\alpha)}\geq n_{w}, so that the arrival constraint in the single-class LP is slack and the work queue is always backlogged.

Normalized capacities.

To express results in comparable units, we normalize all capacities to worker-equivalent units:

H:=μhμw​nh,J:=μjμw​nj,Jeff:=min⁡{nw,J}.H:=\frac{\mu_{h}}{\mu_{w}}\,n_{h},\quad J:=\frac{\mu_{j}}{\mu_{w}}\,n_{j},\quad J_{\mathrm{eff}}:=\min\{n_{w},\,J\}. (31)

Here HH is the rate at which humans can process tasks in worker-output units, JJ is the nominal judge capacity, and JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} is the effective judge capacity. The judge can only process tasks that workers have completed, so its effective capacity is bounded by worker output nwn_{w}; hence Jeff=min⁡{nw,J}J_{\mathrm{eff}}=\min\{n_{w},J\}.

We focus on the regime where the judge improves quality, i.e., qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha. Otherwise the optimal allocation trivially has ϕ∗=0\phi^{*}=0.

Thresholds.

The four phases are separated by three thresholds:

nh(1):=μwμh​ppass​Jeff,nh(2):=μwμh​(nw−prej​Jeff),nh(3):=μwμh​nw.n_{h}^{(1)}:=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}},\quad n_{h}^{(2)}:=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,\big(n_{w}-p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}\big),\quad n_{h}^{(3)}:=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,n_{w}. (32)

The threshold nh(1)n_{h}^{(1)} is the minimum human capacity needed to absorb all judge-filtered output when ϕ=1\phi=1. The threshold nh(2)n_{h}^{(2)} is the human capacity at which workers first become saturated. The threshold nh(3)n_{h}^{(3)} is the human capacity sufficient to absorb all worker output directly, making the judge unnecessary.

Lemma 4.1 (Threshold ordering)

The thresholds satisfy nh(1)≤nh(2)≤nh(3)n_{h}^{(1)}\leq n_{h}^{(2)}\leq n_{h}^{(3)}. If Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w}, then the inequalities are strict.

Proposition 4.2 (Four-phase structure)

Under Assumption 4.1, if qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha and Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w}, then the optimal judge allocation ϕ∗=v∗/x∗\phi^{*}=v^{*}/x^{*} exhibits four phases:

  1. 1.

    If nh≤nh(1)n_{h}\leq n_{h}^{(1)}, then ϕ∗=1\phi^{*}=1 (full screening).

  2. 2.

    If nh(1)≤nh≤nh(2)n_{h}^{(1)}\leq n_{h}\leq n_{h}^{(2)}, then ϕ∗=JeffH+prej​Jeff\displaystyle\phi^{*}=\frac{J_{\mathrm{eff}}}{H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}} (judge saturation).

  3. 3.

    If nh(2)≤nh≤nh(3)n_{h}^{(2)}\leq n_{h}\leq n_{h}^{(3)}, then ϕ∗=nw−Hprej​nw\displaystyle\phi^{*}=\frac{n_{w}-H}{p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,n_{w}} (active reduction).

  4. 4.

    If nh≥nh(3)n_{h}\geq n_{h}^{(3)}, then ϕ∗=0\phi^{*}=0 (judge bypass).

Each phase corresponds to a different binding constraint, and the optimal response differs accordingly.

In Phase 1, humans are the bottleneck. The judge converts one unit of worker output into ppass<1p_{\mathrm{pass}}<1 units of human workload, with the remainder rejected back to workers. This filtering amplifies the effective human capacity: the same number of humans can clear more tasks. The benefit outweighs the rework cost, so the system maximizes judge usage (ϕ∗=1\phi^{*}=1).

In Phase 2, the judge reaches its capacity limit at v∗=Jeffv^{*}=J_{\mathrm{eff}}. Human capacity continues to grow beyond nh(1)n_{h}^{(1)}, but the system cannot route more than JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} through the judge. The additional human capacity must be filled via the direct path, so total worker output x∗x^{*} increases while v∗v^{*} stays fixed. The ratio ϕ∗=v∗/x∗\phi^{*}=v^{*}/x^{*} declines as nhn_{h} grows.

In Phase 3, workers become the bottleneck (x∗=nwx^{*}=n_{w}). Each unit of judge usage now carries a direct opportunity cost: the prejp_{\mathrm{rej}} units of rework compete with new arrivals for scarce worker capacity. To maximize throughput, the system reduces ϕ∗\phi^{*} below the judge-saturated level, trading filtering quality for worker efficiency.

In Phase 4, humans are abundant enough to handle all worker output directly. The judge’s filtering benefit (reducing human load) is no longer needed, but its rework cost persists. The system bypasses the judge entirely.

Illustration (Figure 2a).

Figure 2a plots ϕ∗\phi^{*} and resource utilizations as nhn_{h} varies. The four phases are clearly visible: full screening when humans are scarce (nh≲6n_{h}\lesssim 6), judge saturation (nh≈6n_{h}\approx 6–7.57.5), active reduction of judge usage despite spare capacity (nh≈7.5n_{h}\approx 7.5–1010), and complete judge bypass when humans are abundant (nh≳10n_{h}\gtrsim 10).

Special case: abundant workers.

When worker capacity is large enough to handle both direct flow and maximum rework, Phase 3 vanishes because workers never saturate. Concretely, this requires nw≥H+prej​Jn_{w}\geq H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J, i.e., workers can absorb all direct human flow (HH) plus the maximum rework generated by judge rejections (prej​Jp_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J). Under this condition, the four-phase structure simplifies to two phases.

Proposition 4.3 (Abundant workers)

Under Assumption 4.1, if nw≥H+prej​Jn_{w}\geq H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J and qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha, the optimal judge allocation ϕ∗=v∗/x∗\phi^{*}=v^{*}/x^{*} exhibits two regimes:

  1. 1.

    If H≤ppass​JH\leq p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J, then ϕ∗=1\phi^{*}=1.

  2. 2.

    If H≥ppass​JH\geq p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J, then ϕ∗=JH+prej​J\displaystyle\phi^{*}=\frac{J}{H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J}.

The transition occurs at threshold nh(aw):=μwμh​ppass​Jn_{h}^{(\mathrm{aw})}:=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J.

Below threshold nh(aw)n_{h}^{(\mathrm{aw})}, humans are scarce enough that the system maximizes judge usage (ϕ∗=1\phi^{*}=1). Beyond this threshold, the judge saturates at v∗=Jv^{*}=J while human capacity continues to grow. Total worker output x∗x^{*} increases to fill additional human capacity via the direct path, so ϕ∗=v∗/x∗\phi^{*}=v^{*}/x^{*} declines hyperbolically as ϕ∗∝1/nh\phi^{*}\propto 1/n_{h}. Figure 2b confirms this: beyond threshold nh(aw)≈7n_{h}^{(\mathrm{aw})}\approx 7, ϕ∗\phi^{*} follows a smooth concave curve while all utilizations remain below 100%.

In summary, the operational logic shifts from maximizing judge usage (Phases 1–2) to actively reducing it (Phase 3) to bypassing it entirely (Phase 4), as the bottleneck evolves from humans to workers. When workers are abundant, Phase 3 vanishes and judge usage declines smoothly once the judge saturates.

4.2 Two-Class System: Priority Reversal

Section 4.1 established how to use the judge: a four-phase structure governs the intensity of judge usage as the bottleneck shifts from humans to workers. When tasks are heterogeneous, differing in judge error rates (βi(I),βi(I​I))(\beta_{i}^{(I)},\beta_{i}^{(II)}), a new question arises: which class should receive judge capacity? The single-class phase structure still determines aggregate judge utilization; what changes is the allocation of that capacity across classes. We show that the answer depends on which resource is scarce, and that optimal priority can reverse: the class that should receive judge priority under human scarcity differs from the class prioritized under worker scarcity.

Priority indices.

The optimal class priority is governed by two indices, one for each scarcity regime:

qacc,i=(1−αi)​(1−βi(I))ppass,i,ηi:=βi(I)prej,i.q_{\mathrm{acc},i}=\frac{(1-\alpha_{i})(1-\beta_{i}^{(I)})}{p_{\mathrm{pass},i}},\qquad\eta_{i}:=\frac{\beta_{i}^{(I)}}{p_{\mathrm{rej},i}}. (33)

The index qacc,iq_{\mathrm{acc},i} is the probability that a judge-approved output is correct. When humans are the bottleneck, each unit of human time should yield the highest possible quality, so the system prioritizes the class with higher qacc,iq_{\mathrm{acc},i}.

The index ηi\eta_{i} is the fraction of judge rejections that are false rejections. When workers are the bottleneck, rework is costly: each false rejection consumes worker capacity without correcting an actual error. The class with lower ηi\eta_{i} generates less wasted rework per unit of judge usage, so it is preferred.

{assumption}

[Two-class overloaded regime] We assume symmetric worker parameters μw,1=μw,2=:μw\mu_{w,1}=\mu_{w,2}=:\mu_{w} and α1=α2=:α\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=:\alpha, and that the system is overloaded: λiμw​(1−α)≥nw\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{w}(1-\alpha)}\geq n_{w} for each i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, so that per-class constraints (30b) are slack.

Let kq:=arg⁡maxi∈{1,2}⁡qacc,ik_{q}:=\arg\max_{i\in\{1,2\}}q_{\mathrm{acc},i} and kη:=arg⁡mini∈{1,2}⁡ηik_{\eta}:=\arg\min_{i\in\{1,2\}}\eta_{i} denote the classes favored under human scarcity and worker scarcity, respectively. The nontrivial regime arises when judge capacity is scarce (Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w}, so the system cannot screen all worker outputs and must choose which class to prioritize) and when the two priority indices rank the classes differently (kq≠kηk_{q}\neq k_{\eta}, so one class excels at producing high-quality approved outputs while the other excels at avoiding false rejections). Under these circumstances, the system faces a genuine trade-off between quality and rework as human capacity varies, giving rise to priority reversal. When kq=kηk_{q}=k_{\eta}, the same class dominates both metrics and retains exclusive priority throughout, a degenerate case we set aside. The condition kq≠kηk_{q}\neq k_{\eta} arises naturally in practice: a class with a strict judge (low Type II error β(I​I)\beta^{(II)} but relatively high Type I error β(I)\beta^{(I)}) may achieve high qaccq_{\mathrm{acc}} while simultaneously having high η\eta; conversely, a class with a lenient judge may have low qaccq_{\mathrm{acc}} but also low η\eta.

Proposition 4.4 (Priority reversal)

Under Assumption 4.2, if qacc,i>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc},i}>1-\alpha for both classes, Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w}, and kq≠kηk_{q}\neq k_{\eta}, the following holds. For k∈{1,2}k\in\{1,2\}, let ℓ:=3−k\ell:=3-k.

  1. 1.

    Human-scarce priority. There exists a threshold n¯h>0\underline{n}_{h}>0 such that for all nh≤n¯hn_{h}\leq\underline{n}_{h}, every optimal solution satisfies vkq∗>0v_{k_{q}}^{*}>0 and vℓ∗=0v_{\ell}^{*}=0.

  2. 2.

    Worker-scarce priority. There exists a threshold n¯h\overline{n}_{h} such that for all nh≥n¯hn_{h}\geq\overline{n}_{h}, every optimal solution satisfies vℓ∗=0v_{\ell}^{*}=0; moreover vkη∗>0v_{k_{\eta}}^{*}>0 whenever nh<μwμh​nwn_{h}<\tfrac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,n_{w}.

  3. 3.

    Complementarity. n¯h<n¯h\underline{n}_{h}<\overline{n}_{h}, and there exists a non-degenerate interval I⊂(n¯h,n¯h)I\subset(\underline{n}_{h},\overline{n}_{h}) on which both classes receive strictly positive judge allocation (v1∗>0v_{1}^{*}>0 and v2∗>0v_{2}^{*}>0).

Both thresholds n¯h\underline{n}_{h} and n¯h\overline{n}_{h} admit closed-form expressions in terms of system parameters; see the proof in Appendix 9.5.

The proposition distills optimal multi-class judge allocation into a clean separation of regimes. In the human-scarce regime, each unit of human time is precious, and the system routes judge capacity to the class whose approved outputs are most likely correct (highest qaccq_{\mathrm{acc}}), ensuring that humans see the highest-quality work. In the worker-scarce regime, rework is the primary cost, and the system routes judge capacity to the class with the lowest false-rejection rate (lowest η\eta), preserving worker capacity for new production.

The complementarity zone reflects the fact that concentrating judge capacity on a single class is not always optimal. Suppose we allocate all judge capacity to class kqk_{q} (highest qaccq_{\mathrm{acc}}), which produces the highest-quality screened outputs. Because judge capacity is limited, only a portion of tasks can be screened; the remainder bypass the judge and go directly to human review at lower quality. If human capacity is not fully utilized by the screened outputs from class kqk_{q} alone, the slack is filled by unscreened work. Now consider diverting some judge capacity to the other class, which has lower η\eta (fewer false rejections). This class produces “medium-quality” screened outputs at a higher rate per unit of judge capacity. The result is a portfolio of “high-quality plus medium-quality” screened work, which can dominate the original “high-quality plus low-quality (unscreened)” mix. In the complementarity zone, this rebalancing strictly improves throughput: sharing judge capacity across both classes yields better overall performance than concentrating it on either one.

Illustration (Figure 3).

Figure 3 plots the optimal judge allocation for two classes as nhn_{h} varies, with Class 1 having a lenient judge (β1(I)=0.05\beta_{1}^{(I)}=0.05, β1(I​I)=0.40\beta_{1}^{(II)}=0.40) and Class 2 having a stricter judge (β2(I)=0.15\beta_{2}^{(I)}=0.15, β2(I​I)=0.10\beta_{2}^{(II)}=0.10). Here Class 2 has higher qaccq_{\mathrm{acc}} (better quality conditioned on acceptance) but also higher η\eta (more false rejections), so kq=2k_{q}=2 and kη=1k_{\eta}=1: the two indices disagree, producing a priority reversal. As predicted by the proposition: for small nhn_{h}, all judge capacity goes to Class 2 (human-scarce priority); for large nhn_{h} approaching μwμh​nw\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}n_{w}, judge capacity shifts entirely to Class 1 (worker-scarce priority). The reversal is not abrupt: the complementarity zone provides a smooth transition where Class 2’s allocation gradually decreases while Class 1’s allocation gradually increases, with both classes sharing judge capacity during this intermediate regime.

In summary, optimal judge allocation in multi-class systems is governed by a simple structural principle: priority is determined by qaccq_{\mathrm{acc}} when humans are scarce and by η\eta when workers are scarce. When these two indices disagree on which class should be prioritized, the system must reverse its priority as operating conditions change, with a complementarity zone smoothing the transition. All thresholds are computable in closed form from system parameters (Proposition 4.4), enabling direct implementation.

5 Stochastic Control Policy

The steady-state analysis in Sections 3–4 characterizes optimal judge allocation and resource utilization for the fluid model. This section translates these insights into an implementable control policy for the stochastic nn-system, establishing asymptotic optimality as the system scale grows.

5.1 The Fluid-Tracking Policy

The policy has two components: (i) an inspection rule that determines the probability of routing completed work to the judge, and (ii) an admission rule that regulates which tasks enter worker service. Both components are derived directly from the LP solution.

Inspection rule.

Given an optimal solution (qw,i∗,xi∗,yi∗,zi,d∗,zi,j∗,vi∗)i∈ℐ(q_{w,i}^{*},x_{i}^{*},y_{i}^{*},z_{i,d}^{*},z_{i,j}^{*},v_{i}^{*})_{i\in\mathcal{I}} to the steady-state fluid LP (29), define the inspection rate for each class ii as

ϕi∗:=vi∗/xi∗if ​xi∗>0,ϕi∗:=0if ​xi∗=0.\phi_{i}^{*}:=v_{i}^{*}/x_{i}^{*}\quad\text{if }x_{i}^{*}>0,\qquad\phi_{i}^{*}:=0\quad\text{if }x_{i}^{*}=0. (34)

Whenever an AI-Worker completes service on a class-ii task, route the output to the judge for screening with probability ϕi∗\phi_{i}^{*}; otherwise, forward it directly to human review. This probabilistic routing ensures that the long-run fraction of class-ii outputs sent to the judge matches the fluid-optimal allocation vi∗/xi∗v_{i}^{*}/x_{i}^{*}.

The inspection rate ϕi∗\phi_{i}^{*} encodes the trade-off identified in Section 4: higher ϕi∗\phi_{i}^{*} increases judge utilization and reduces human load through rejection filtering, but also increases Type I rework. The LP solution balances these effects optimally for each class.

Admission rule.

Let Qw,in​(t)Q_{w,i}^{n}(t) denote the number of class-ii tasks waiting in the work queue at time tt, and let Xin​(t)X_{i}^{n}(t) denote the number currently in AI-Worker service. When worker capacity becomes available, a class ii is admissible at time tt if

Xin​(t−)​<n​xi∗andQw,in​(t−)>​0.X_{i}^{n}(t^{-})<n\,x_{i}^{*}\quad\text{and}\quad Q_{w,i}^{n}(t^{-})>0. (35)

If multiple classes are admissible, select one according to any work-conserving rule (e.g., FCFS across classes, round-robin, or maximum queue deviation from target). The policy is work-conserving whenever ∑iXin​(t−)<n​∑ixi∗\sum_{i}X_{i}^{n}(t^{-})<n\sum_{i}x_{i}^{*} and ∑iQw,in​(t−)>0\sum_{i}Q_{w,i}^{n}(t^{-})>0; idling occurs only when all classes have reached their target in-service levels. The judge and human pools operate under work-conserving FCFS scheduling.

The threshold condition Xin​(t)<n​xi∗X_{i}^{n}(t)<n\,x_{i}^{*} is the key mechanism for achieving steady-state optimality. It prevents over-admission to any single class and ensures that worker capacity is reserved for rework traffic. Without this threshold, a naive policy might saturate workers with new arrivals, leaving no capacity for tasks that require reprocessing after judge rejection or human correction.

5.2 Asymptotic Optimality

We now establish that the Fluid-Tracking policy achieves the fluid-optimal throughput as the system scale grows. Let Cin​(T)C_{i}^{n}(T) denote the cumulative number of class-ii tasks successfully completed (accepted by human reviewers) by time TT in the nn-system.

Theorem 5.1 (Asymptotic optimality)

Let R∗R^{*} denote the optimal value of the steady-state fluid LP (29), and let Assumption 3 hold. Under the Fluid-Tracking policy 𝛑n,∗\bm{\pi}^{n,*}:

lim infT→∞lim infn→∞1n​T​𝔼𝝅n,∗​[∑i∈ℐri​Cin​(T)]=R∗.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\;\liminf_{n\to\infty}\;\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\bm{\pi}^{n,*}}\Big[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}\,C_{i}^{n}(T)\Big]\;=\;R^{*}. (36)

The inner limit (n→∞n\to\infty) invokes the fluid approximation on a fixed horizon [0,T][0,T]; the outer limit (T→∞T\to\infty) captures the long-run average. The proof follows the standard fluid-limit methodology: show that the stochastic system, when scaled by 1/n1/n, converges to the deterministic fluid model; then verify that the Fluid-Tracking policy drives the fluid trajectory to the optimal steady state. The threshold condition (35) ensures that binding capacity constraints are satisfied with equality in the limit, while the inspection rate (34) ensures optimal flow splitting between the judge and direct paths.

6 Extensions

The baseline model assumes that AI-Worker error rates remain constant and that AI capacities are exogenously fixed. This section relaxes both assumptions. Section 6.1 models how human feedback from rejected tasks improves the AI-Worker’s success probability on rework, altering the optimal routing policy. Section 6.2 treats AI-Worker and LLM-Judge capacities as decision variables subject to a budget constraint, enabling joint optimization of capacity allocation and operational control.

6.1 Human Feedback Improves Success Probability

When human review rejects a task, the accompanying feedback helps the AI-Worker improve upon rework. This section extends the baseline model to capture this learning effect. We proceed in four steps: (i) define the extended state space and flow dynamics, (ii) derive the steady-state LP for a single class, (iii) extend to multiple classes, and (iv) establish an asymptotically optimal control policy.

Model setup.

We distinguish fresh tasks, which have failure rate α\alpha and judge routing fraction ϕ\phi, from feedback tasks, which have reduced failure rate κ​α\kappa\alpha for some κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) and routing fraction ϕf​b\phi_{fb}. Feedback tasks that fail a second time are removed from the system to ensure finite rework cycles, and judge-rejected tasks return to the fresh pool since no human feedback is received.

At the stochastic level, we duplicate all state processes for the two task types. For fresh tasks: Qwn​(t)Q_{w}^{n}(t) (work queue), Xn​(t)X^{n}(t) (in worker service), Qjn​(t)Q_{j}^{n}(t) (judge queue), Yn​(t)Y^{n}(t) (in judge service), Qhn​(t)Q_{h}^{n}(t) (human queue), and Zn​(t)Z^{n}(t) (in human service). For feedback tasks, we use the subscript f​bfb: Qw,f​bn​(t)Q_{w,fb}^{n}(t), Xf​bn​(t)X_{fb}^{n}(t), Qj,f​bn​(t)Q_{j,fb}^{n}(t), Yf​bn​(t)Y_{fb}^{n}(t), Qh,f​bn​(t)Q_{h,fb}^{n}(t), and Zf​bn​(t)Z_{fb}^{n}(t). Fresh tasks arrive exogenously and from judge rejections; feedback tasks arrive from human rejections of fresh tasks. At the fluid level, we use lowercase: (qw,x,qj,y,qh,z)(q_{w},x,q_{j},y,q_{h},z) for fresh and (qw,f​b,xf​b,qj,f​b,yf​b,qh,f​b,zf​b)(q_{w,fb},x_{fb},q_{j,fb},y_{fb},q_{h,fb},z_{fb}) for feedback. The judge-routed worker service levels are v:=ϕ​xv:=\phi x for fresh and vf​b:=ϕf​b​xf​bv_{fb}:=\phi_{fb}x_{fb} for feedback.

Single-class steady-state LP.

The flow balance linking the two task types follows from the observation that feedback tasks are generated by human rejections of fresh tasks. Since ppass=(1−α)​(1−β(I))+α​β(I​I)p_{\mathrm{pass}}=(1-\alpha)(1-\beta^{(I)})+\alpha\beta^{(II)} and qacc=(1−α)​(1−β(I))/ppassq_{\mathrm{acc}}=(1-\alpha)(1-\beta^{(I)})/p_{\mathrm{pass}}, we have ppass​(1−qacc)=ppass−(1−α)​(1−β(I))=α​β(I​I)p_{\mathrm{pass}}(1-q_{\mathrm{acc}})=p_{\mathrm{pass}}-(1-\alpha)(1-\beta^{(I)})=\alpha\beta^{(II)}. Using this identity, the feedback task service level satisfies xf​b=α⁡(x−(1−β(I​I))​v)x_{fb}=\alpha(x-(1-\beta^{(II)})v). The judge rejection probability for feedback tasks is prej,f​b:=(1−κ​α)​β(I)+κ​α​(1−β(I​I))p_{\mathrm{rej},fb}:=(1-\kappa\alpha)\beta^{(I)}+\kappa\alpha(1-\beta^{(II)}). Applying the same variable elimination as in Section 3, the steady-state LP becomes

maxx,v,xf​b,vf​b\displaystyle\max_{x,v,x_{fb},v_{fb}}\quad μw​[(1−α)​(x−β(I)​v)+(1−κ​α)​(xf​b−β(I)​vf​b)]\displaystyle\mu_{w}\Big[(1-\alpha)(x-\beta^{(I)}v)+(1-\kappa\alpha)(x_{fb}-\beta^{(I)}v_{fb})\Big] (37a)
s.t. xf​b=α⁡(x−(1−β(I​I))​v),0≤v≤x,0≤vf​b≤xf​b,\displaystyle x_{fb}=\alpha\big(x-(1-\beta^{(II)})v\big),\quad 0\leq v\leq x,\quad 0\leq v_{fb}\leq x_{fb}, (37b)
x+xf​b≤nw,μwμj​(v+vf​b)≤nj,\displaystyle x+x_{fb}\leq n_{w},\quad\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{j}}(v+v_{fb})\leq n_{j}, (37c)
μwμh​[(x−prej​v)+(xf​b−prej,f​b​vf​b)]≤nh.\displaystyle\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\big[(x-p_{\mathrm{rej}}v)+(x_{fb}-p_{\mathrm{rej},fb}v_{fb})\big]\leq n_{h}. (37d)

We next state two structural properties of LP (37). The first shows that feedback tasks do not build a steady-state queue at optimality. The second characterizes how scarce judge capacity is allocated between fresh and feedback tasks.

Proposition 6.1 (Feedback queue vanishes in steady state)

In the feedback model (37), any optimal solution satisfies xf​b∗=α⁡(x∗−(1−β(I​I))​v∗)x_{fb}^{*}=\alpha(x^{*}-(1-\beta^{(II)})v^{*}); that is, the feedback flow-balance constraint (37b) holds with equality, implying zero feedback-queue mass in steady state.

The key point is that feedback arrivals are endogenous: feedback tasks are created only when humans reject fresh tasks. If a positive feedback queue formed in steady state, then some feedback tasks would abandon, reducing feedback throughput. Since the objective is strictly increasing in completed feedback tasks, any solution permitting such losses is suboptimal; the optimizer maintains qw,f​b∗=0q_{w,fb}^{*}=0.

Proposition 6.2 (Judge priority under feedback)

Consider the feedback model (37) with κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) and qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha. Suppose the judge and human constraints bind while the worker constraint is slack (v∗+vf​b∗=Jeffv^{*}+v_{fb}^{*}=J_{\mathrm{eff}}, x∗+xf​b∗<nwx^{*}+x_{fb}^{*}<n_{w}). Then:

  1. (i)

    If

    1−β(I​I)>(1−β(I)−β(I​I))​(α2​κ+α),1-\beta^{(II)}>(1-\beta^{(I)}-\beta^{(II)})(\alpha^{2}\kappa+\alpha), (38)

    then fresh-first is optimal: vf​b∗>0⇒ϕ∗=1v_{fb}^{*}>0\Rightarrow\phi^{*}=1.

  2. (ii)

    If the strict reverse of (38) holds, then feedback-first is optimal: v∗>0⇒ϕf​b∗=1v^{*}>0\Rightarrow\phi_{fb}^{*}=1.

The intuition is as follows. The left-hand side of (38), 1−β(I​I)1-\beta^{(II)}, is the judge’s probability of catching an incorrect output. The right-hand side has a concrete two-layer interpretation. The term (1−β(I)−β(I​I))=(1−β(I​I))−β(I)(1-\beta^{(I)}-\beta^{(II)})=(1-\beta^{(II)})-\beta^{(I)} measures how informative a rejection decision is, because it is the excess probability of rejecting wrong outputs over mistakenly rejecting correct ones. The factor α+κ​α2=α⁡(1+α​κ)\alpha+\kappa\alpha^{2}=\alpha(1+\alpha\kappa) summarizes the strength of error propagation through the feedback loop: a fraction α\alpha of fresh tasks are wrong, and feedback tasks are still wrong with probability κ​α\kappa\alpha, so the second-round error mass scales as κ​α2\kappa\alpha^{2}.

When judge and human are both binding and worker capacity is slack, a marginal unit of judge capacity should be used where it reduces expected human workload the most. Condition (38) is both necessary and sufficient for fresh-first priority: when it holds, allocating judge capacity to fresh tasks yields a strictly larger net human-load reduction than allocating it to feedback tasks. When it fails (strict inequality reversed), the opposite is true: screening fresh tasks too aggressively reduces human rejections and thereby shrinks the supply of feedback tasks. In that regime, the optimal policy allocates judge capacity to feedback tasks first, letting some fresh tasks bypass the judge to generate feedback while using the judge to protect the human bottleneck from feedback errors.

Figure 4 illustrates these structural properties for κ=0.5\kappa=0.5. The left panel decomposes judge utilization into the fresh and feedback components as nhn_{h} varies. It shows that the phase structure from the baseline model persists, but the two task types compete for the same judge capacity, so the composition of judge load matters. The right panel plots the optimal routing fractions (ϕ∗,ϕf​b∗)(\phi^{*},\phi_{fb}^{*}) and provides a visual illustration of Proposition 6.2: when judge capacity saturates, fresh tasks keep full judge routing while feedback tasks begin to bypass the judge.

Multi-class steady-state LP.

The single-class analysis reveals two key structural properties: feedback queues vanish in steady state, and judge capacity prioritizes fresh tasks when judge and human are both binding and worker capacity is slack. We now generalize to multiple classes, where each class may have different feedback effectiveness.

We extend to multiple classes i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, each with feedback effectiveness κi∈(0,1)\kappa_{i}\in(0,1). The state processes are duplicated for fresh and feedback tasks within each class, following the single-class structure. Denoting the net completion rate of fresh and feedback tasks by Ti:=(1−αi)​(xi−βi(I)​vi)T_{i}:=(1-\alpha_{i})(x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}) and Ti,f​b:=(1−κi​αi)​(xi,f​b−βi(I)​vi,f​b)T_{i,fb}:=(1-\kappa_{i}\alpha_{i})(x_{i,fb}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i,fb}), the multi-class steady-state LP is:

max{xi,vi,xi,f​b,vi,f​b}\displaystyle\max_{\{x_{i},v_{i},x_{i,fb},v_{i,fb}\}}\quad ∑i∈ℐri​μw,i​(Ti+Ti,f​b)\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}\,\mu_{w,i}(T_{i}+T_{i,fb}) (39a)
s.t. xi,f​b=αi​(xi−(1−βi(I​I))​vi),  0≤vi≤xi,  0≤vi,f​b≤xi,f​b,\displaystyle x_{i,fb}=\alpha_{i}(x_{i}-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}),\;\;0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i},\;\;0\leq v_{i,fb}\leq x_{i,fb}, ∀i∈ℐ,\displaystyle\forall i\in\mathcal{I}, (39b)
∑i∈ℐ(xi+xi,f​b)≤nw,∑i∈ℐμw,iμj,i​(vi+vi,f​b)≤nj,\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}(x_{i}+x_{i,fb})\leq n_{w},\quad\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}(v_{i}+v_{i,fb})\leq n_{j}, (39c)
∑i∈ℐμw,iμh,i​[(xi−prej,i​vi)+(xi,f​b−prej,i,f​b​vi,f​b)]≤nh.\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{h,i}}\big[(x_{i}-p_{\mathrm{rej},i}v_{i})+(x_{i,fb}-p_{\mathrm{rej},i,fb}v_{i,fb})\big]\leq n_{h}. (39d)

The structural insights from the single-class case extend naturally: within each class, feedback queues vanish in steady state, and judge capacity prioritizes fresh tasks over feedback tasks when judge and human are both binding and worker capacity is slack.

Fluid-Tracking policy for feedback model.

We now translate the LP solution into an implementable stochastic control policy. Given an optimal solution (xi∗,vi∗,xi,f​b∗,vi,f​b∗)i∈ℐ(x_{i}^{*},v_{i}^{*},x_{i,fb}^{*},v_{i,fb}^{*})_{i\in\mathcal{I}} to LP (39), define the Fluid-Tracking policy 𝝅n,f​b\bm{\pi}^{n,fb} as follows.

Admission rule. For each class ii, define the aggregate worker threshold as n⁡(xi∗+xi,f​b∗)n(x_{i}^{*}+x_{i,fb}^{*}). A fresh task of class ii is admissible at time tt if

Xin​(t−)+Xi,f​bn​(t−)​<n⁡(xi∗+xi,f​b∗)andQw,in​(t−)>​0.X_{i}^{n}(t^{-})+X_{i,fb}^{n}(t^{-})<n(x_{i}^{*}+x_{i,fb}^{*})\quad\text{and}\quad Q_{w,i}^{n}(t^{-})>0.

A feedback task of class ii is admissible if

Xin​(t−)+Xi,f​bn​(t−)​<n⁡(xi∗+xi,f​b∗)andQw,i,f​bn​(t−)>​0.X_{i}^{n}(t^{-})+X_{i,fb}^{n}(t^{-})<n(x_{i}^{*}+x_{i,fb}^{*})\quad\text{and}\quad Q_{w,i,fb}^{n}(t^{-})>0.

When worker capacity becomes available, feedback tasks have priority over fresh tasks: among admissible tasks, admit feedback tasks first. This priority rule is consistent with Proposition 6.1: since qw,i,f​b∗=0q_{w,i,fb}^{*}=0 in the optimal fluid solution, the stochastic policy should ensure feedback tasks do not accumulate.

Routing rule. Define the inspection rates ϕi∗:=vi∗/xi∗\phi_{i}^{*}:=v_{i}^{*}/x_{i}^{*} for fresh tasks and ϕi,f​b∗:=vi,f​b∗/xi,f​b∗\phi_{i,fb}^{*}:=v_{i,fb}^{*}/x_{i,fb}^{*} for feedback tasks (with the convention 0/0:=00/0:=0). When a fresh task of class ii completes worker service, route it to the judge with probability ϕi∗\phi_{i}^{*}; otherwise route directly to human review. When a feedback task of class ii completes worker service, route it to the judge with probability ϕi,f​b∗\phi_{i,fb}^{*}.

Theorem 6.3 (Asymptotic optimality under feedback)

Let Rf​b∗R_{fb}^{*} denote the optimal value of LP (39), and let Cin​(T)C_{i}^{n}(T) and Ci,f​bn​(T)C_{i,fb}^{n}(T) denote the cumulative completions of fresh and feedback tasks of class ii by time TT. Under the Fluid-Tracking policy 𝛑n,f​b\bm{\pi}^{n,fb}:

lim infT→∞lim infn→∞1n​T​𝔼𝝅n,f​b​[∑i∈ℐri​(Cin​(T)+Ci,f​bn​(T))]=Rf​b∗.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\;\liminf_{n\to\infty}\;\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\bm{\pi}^{n,fb}}\Big[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}\,\big(C_{i}^{n}(T)+C_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big)\Big]\;=\;R_{fb}^{*}. (40)

6.2 Capacity Planning for AI Resources

In practice, AI-Worker and LLM-Judge capacities are not fixed but can be scaled by allocating computational resources. This section studies the joint optimization of capacity allocation (nw,nj)(n_{w},n_{j}) and operational control (xi,vi)(x_{i},v_{i}) when the total AI resource budget γw​nw+γj​nj≤B\gamma_{w}n_{w}+\gamma_{j}n_{j}\leq B is constrained, where γw,γj>0\gamma_{w},\gamma_{j}>0 are unit costs and B>0B>0 is the budget. Human capacity nhn_{h} is treated as fixed. Adding the budget constraint to the baseline LP yields:

maxnw,nj,{xi,vi}\displaystyle\max_{n_{w},n_{j},\{x_{i},v_{i}\}}\quad ∑i∈ℐri​μw,i​(1−αi)​(xi−βi(I)​vi)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}r_{i}\mu_{w,i}(1-\alpha_{i})(x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}) (41a)
s.t. γw​nw+γj​nj≤B,0≤vi≤xi​∀i,\displaystyle\gamma_{w}n_{w}+\gamma_{j}n_{j}\leq B,\quad 0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i}\;\;\forall i, (41b)
∑ixi≤nw,∑iμw,iμj,i​vi≤nj,\displaystyle\sum_{i}x_{i}\leq n_{w},\quad\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}v_{i}\leq n_{j}, (41c)
∑iμw,iμh,i​(xi−prej,i​vi)≤nh.\displaystyle\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{h,i}}(x_{i}-p_{\mathrm{rej},i}v_{i})\leq n_{h}. (41d)

The key structural insight is that worker and judge capacities are coupled through the budget.

Proposition 6.4 (Worker-Judge coupling)

In LP (41) with qacc,i>1−αiq_{\mathrm{acc},i}>1-\alpha_{i} for all ii, if the human constraint binds, then there exists an optimal solution in which the worker and judge constraints are either both binding or both slack.

Intuitively, the budget constraint couples worker and judge capacities: spending more on one means spending less on the other. When humans are the bottleneck, the system invests in judge capacity to filter tasks and reduce human load; as humans become abundant, the system shifts budget from judges to workers to maximize throughput. Figure 5(a) illustrates this trade-off.

The right panel of Figure 5 demonstrates the value of capacity planning by comparing throughput against fixed allocation strategies. With capacity planning, throughput increases monotonically with nhn_{h} as the system dynamically reallocates budget from judges to workers. In contrast, fixed allocations perform well only in specific regimes: a balanced allocation (nw,nj)=(5,5)(n_{w},n_{j})=(5,5) works when humans are scarce but plateaus early; a worker-heavy allocation (7,3)(7,3) extends the range but still saturates; and a pure-worker allocation (10,0)(10,0) underperforms when humans are scarce (lacking filtering capability) but catches up when humans are abundant. Capacity planning dominates across all nhn_{h} by adapting the resource mix to the prevailing bottleneck.

For implementation, the capacity planning problem decouples into two stages: first solve LP (41) to obtain (nw∗,nj∗)(n_{w}^{*},n_{j}^{*}), then apply the Fluid-Tracking policy from Section 5.1 with the planned capacities. We implement planned capacities as integers: nwn=⌊n⋅nw∗⌋n_{w}^{n}=\lfloor n\cdot n_{w}^{*}\rfloor and njn=⌊n⋅nj∗⌋n_{j}^{n}=\lfloor n\cdot n_{j}^{*}\rfloor. This preserves feasibility of the fluid targets up to O⁡(1)O(1) rounding error; stability is maintained by the admission control component of the Fluid-Tracking policy.

7 Numerical Experiments

This section validates the Fluid-Tracking policy through discrete-event simulation. We examine two aspects: (i) convergence to fluid-optimal throughput as system scale increases, and (ii) comparison with baseline policies that lack either admission control or optimal routing.

7.1 Asymptotic Optimality

We verify that the optimality gap between the Fluid-Tracking policy and the LP upper bound vanishes as the system scale nn grows.

Experimental setup.

We generate 20 random problem instances, each with 3–5 task classes. For each instance, the parameters are drawn independently: error rate αi∼Uniform⁡(0.20,0.35)\alpha_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0.20,0.35), Type I error βi(I)∼Uniform⁡(0.05,0.15)\beta_{i}^{(I)}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0.05,0.15), Type II error βi(I​I)∼Uniform⁡(0.10,0.25)\beta_{i}^{(II)}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0.10,0.25), service rates μw,i∼Uniform⁡(18,22)\mu_{w,i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(18,22), μj,i∼Uniform⁡(28,32)\mu_{j,i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(28,32), μh,i∼Uniform⁡(9,11)\mu_{h,i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(9,11), arrival rate λi∼Uniform⁡(50,70)\lambda_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(50,70), and abandonment rate θi∼Uniform⁡(0.4,0.6)\theta_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0.4,0.6). Base capacities are nw∼Uniform⁡(4,6)n_{w}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(4,6), nj∼Uniform⁡(2,4)n_{j}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(2,4), and nh∼Uniform⁡(5,8)n_{h}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(5,8). Reward weights are ri=1r_{i}=1 for all classes. For each instance and scale factor n∈{1,2,5,10,20,50}n\in\{1,2,5,10,20,50\}, we run 5 independent replications with different random seeds. Each replication simulates 500 time units with a 100-unit warmup period. We compute the optimality gap for each (instance, seed) pair and report the mean and standard deviation across all 100 runs at each scale nn.

The optimality gap is defined as (R∗−Rsim)/R∗×100%(R^{*}-R_{\mathrm{sim}})/R^{*}\times 100\%, where R∗R^{*} is the LP optimal value and RsimR_{\mathrm{sim}} is the simulated throughput.

Results.

Figure 6 shows the optimality gap across all instances and seeds. The mean gap decreases from 0.69% at n=1n=1 to below 0.1% for n≥10n\geq 10. The variance also decreases substantially: the standard deviation drops from 0.95% at n=1n=1 to 0.08% at n=50n=50. This confirms the theoretical prediction that the Fluid-Tracking policy achieves asymptotic optimality. Even at the smallest scale (n=1n=1), the mean gap remains below 1%, suggesting that the fluid-based policy provides reasonable guidance even for moderately sized systems. The small residual gap at large nn reflects finite-horizon effects and discrete rounding in capacity allocation.

7.2 Policy Comparison

We compare the Fluid-Tracking policy against three baseline policies that represent common practical approaches. All baselines use greedy admission (admit any waiting task when capacity is available), but differ in routing:

  • •

    Greedy + Optimal: Uses the LP-optimal routing fractions ϕi∗\phi_{i}^{*}, but without admission control thresholds.

  • •

    Greedy + Always-Judge: Routes all tasks through the judge (ϕi=1\phi_{i}=1).

  • •

    Greedy + Never-Judge: Bypasses the judge entirely (ϕi=0\phi_{i}=0).

Experimental setup.

We use the two-class instance from Section 4.2: λi=75\lambda_{i}=75, α=0.3\alpha=0.3, (β1(I),β1(I​I))=(0.05,0.40)(\beta_{1}^{(I)},\beta_{1}^{(II)})=(0.05,0.40), (β2(I),β2(I​I))=(0.15,0.10)(\beta_{2}^{(I)},\beta_{2}^{(II)})=(0.15,0.10), (μw,μj,μh)=(20,30,10)(\mu_{w},\mu_{j},\mu_{h})=(20,30,10), nw=10n_{w}=10, nj=6n_{j}=6, and θi=0.5\theta_{i}=0.5. Human capacity nhn_{h} varies from 3 to 22 to cover all four phases. The system is scaled by n=10n=10, and each configuration runs for 250 time units with a 50-unit warmup. We report the average over 3 seeds.

A policy is classified as unstable if the judge queue QjQ_{j} or human queue QhQ_{h} exhibits linear growth. Specifically, we fit a linear regression to the queue trajectory over the latter half of the simulation; if R2>0.9R^{2}>0.9 and the slope exceeds 1.0 per unit time, the policy is deemed unstable. These thresholds are heuristic; qualitative conclusions are robust to moderate changes in the cutoff values.

Results: Throughput and stability.

Figure 7 compares throughput across policies as nhn_{h} varies. The Fluid-Tracking policy achieves the highest throughput and remains stable across all nhn_{h}. In contrast:

The Greedy + Optimal policy matches Fluid-Tracking throughput but is generically unstable across all values of nhn_{h}. Without admission control, it over-admits tasks, causing queues to grow unboundedly. This illustrates that optimal routing alone is insufficient; admission control is essential for stability.

The Always-Judge policy saturates at a lower throughput for nh≥13n_{h}\geq 13. By routing all tasks through the judge, it creates a bottleneck at the judge queue, which grows without bound.

The Never-Judge policy performs poorly when humans are scarce (nh<10n_{h}<10) because it sends all worker outputs, including errors, directly to humans. As nhn_{h} increases, its throughput converges to the Fluid-Tracking level, since the optimal policy itself bypasses the judge when human capacity is abundant (Phase 4). However, greedy admission still causes instability at intermediate nhn_{h} values.

Results: Queue trajectories.

Figure 8 shows queue trajectories at nh=14n_{h}=14, a regime where human capacity is moderate. The Fluid-Tracking policy maintains bounded queues throughout the simulation, with both QjQ_{j} and QhQ_{h} fluctuating around low levels. All three baseline policies exhibit linear queue growth: Greedy + Optimal and Never-Judge cause human queue explosion, while Always-Judge causes judge queue explosion.

These trajectories illustrate the distinct failure modes. Greedy admission without thresholds admits tasks faster than the system can process them, leading to queue buildup at the downstream bottleneck. The routing choice determines which queue explodes: Always-Judge overloads the judge, while optimal routing and Never-Judge overload humans.

In summary, the Fluid-Tracking policy achieves near-optimal throughput with vanishing gap as scale increases, and both admission control and adaptive routing are necessary: policies using only one component fail to maintain stability across operating regimes.

8 Conclusion

The value of LLM-judge screening in AI-human workflows depends on which resource constrains the system, not on judge accuracy alone. This paper developed a framework for optimal judge allocation that makes this precise: judge screening is neither universally beneficial nor universally harmful. When humans are scarce, screening amplifies their effective capacity. When workers are scarce, screening generates rework that crowds out new production. The closed-form thresholds we derive allow practitioners to determine which regime they operate in and to set routing policies accordingly.

The analysis reveals that optimal control of AI-human systems requires reasoning about feedback loops and capacity interactions, not just component-level accuracy metrics. A high-accuracy judge can reduce throughput if deployed in the wrong regime, while a moderate-accuracy judge can improve throughput if it relieves the binding constraint. This observation has broader implications for how organizations evaluate and deploy AI components: system-level performance depends on how components interact under resource constraints, not only on how each component performs in isolation.

Several directions remain open. First, extending the framework to contextual routing, where decisions condition on task-specific covariates rather than discrete classes, would enable finer-grained control, connecting to the contextual bandits literature. Second, allowing heterogeneous resource pools, where different agents have different error rates or specializations, would introduce assignment decisions alongside routing, potentially yielding richer structure when agent and task heterogeneity interact. Third, relaxing the binary quality model to continuous quality scores and the infallible human assumption to imperfect human review would create more realistic settings where screening stringency and cognitive load interact. Finally, modeling learning judges whose accuracy improves via operational feedback creates a joint learning-and-control problem, connecting to the growing literature on learning in service systems.

9 Proofs of Main Results

9.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Fluid Limit)

Proof 9.1

proof: Fix T>0T>0 and denote W¯n:=Wn/n\bar{W}^{n}:=W^{n}/n for any process WnW^{n}. The primitive counting processes are time-changed Poisson processes:

Ain​(t)\displaystyle A_{i}^{n}(t) =Na,i​(λi​n​t),Bw,in​(t)=Nb,i​(∫0tθi​Qw,in​(s)​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{a,i}(\lambda_{i}nt),\quad B_{w,i}^{n}(t)=N_{b,i}\Big(\int_{0}^{t}\theta_{i}Q_{w,i}^{n}(s)\,ds\Big),
Dw,in​(t)\displaystyle D_{w,i}^{n}(t) =Ndw,i​(∫0tμw,i​Xin​(s)​𝑑s),Dj,in​(t)=Ndj,i​(∫0tμj,i​Yin​(s)​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{d_{w},i}\Big(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}X_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds\Big),\quad D_{j,i}^{n}(t)=N_{d_{j},i}\Big(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{j,i}Y_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds\Big),
Dh,in​(t)\displaystyle D_{h,i}^{n}(t) =Ndh,i​(∫0tμh,i​(Zi,dn​(s)+Zi,jn​(s))​𝑑s),\displaystyle=N_{d_{h},i}\Big(\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{h,i}(Z_{i,d}^{n}(s)+Z_{i,j}^{n}(s))\,ds\Big),

where {N⋅​(⋅)}\{N_{\cdot}(\cdot)\} are independent unit-rate Poisson processes.

Tightness.

Define the time-change functions Λw,in​(t):=∫0tμw,i​Xin​(s)​𝑑s\Lambda_{w,i}^{n}(t):=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}X_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds and similarly for other service processes. The capacity constraints give ∑iXin​(s)≤n​nw\sum_{i}X_{i}^{n}(s)\leq n\,n_{w}, ∑iYin​(s)≤n​nj\sum_{i}Y_{i}^{n}(s)\leq n\,n_{j}, and ∑i(Zi,dn+Zi,jn)​(s)≤n​nh\sum_{i}(Z_{i,d}^{n}+Z_{i,j}^{n})(s)\leq n\,n_{h}. Hence

1n​Λw,in​(t)≤μw,i​nw​t,1n​Λj,in​(t)≤μj,i​nj​t,1n​Λh,in​(t)≤μh,i​nh​t.\frac{1}{n}\Lambda_{w,i}^{n}(t)\leq\mu_{w,i}\,n_{w}\,t,\quad\frac{1}{n}\Lambda_{j,i}^{n}(t)\leq\mu_{j,i}\,n_{j}\,t,\quad\frac{1}{n}\Lambda_{h,i}^{n}(t)\leq\mu_{h,i}\,n_{h}\,t.

For the abandonment time-change, since Qw,in​(s)≤Qw,in​(0)+Ain​(s)Q_{w,i}^{n}(s)\leq Q_{w,i}^{n}(0)+A_{i}^{n}(s), we have 1n​∫0tθi​Qw,in​(s)​𝑑s≤θi​(t​Q¯w,in​(0)+t​A¯in​(t))\frac{1}{n}\int_{0}^{t}\theta_{i}Q_{w,i}^{n}(s)\,ds\leq\theta_{i}(t\,\bar{Q}_{w,i}^{n}(0)+t\,\bar{A}_{i}^{n}(t)). By the functional strong law of large numbers (FSLLN), A¯in​(t)=Na,i​(λi​n​t)/n→λi​t\bar{A}_{i}^{n}(t)=N_{a,i}(\lambda_{i}nt)/n\to\lambda_{i}t uniformly on [0,T][0,T] almost surely. Combined with Assumption 3, the scaled time-changes are stochastically bounded on [0,T][0,T].

For the scaled counting processes, since Λw,in​(t)≤μw,i​n​nw​t\Lambda_{w,i}^{n}(t)\leq\mu_{w,i}n\,n_{w}\,t, we have Ndw,i​(Λw,in​(t))/n≤Ndw,i​(μw,i​n​nw​t)/nN_{d_{w},i}(\Lambda_{w,i}^{n}(t))/n\leq N_{d_{w},i}(\mu_{w,i}n\,n_{w}\,t)/n, and the latter is tight by FSLLN. The same bound applies to all other time-changed Poisson coordinates. The admission controls U⋅,inU_{\cdot,i}^{n} are nondecreasing with Uw,in​(t)≤Qw,in​(0)+Ain​(t)U_{w,i}^{n}(t)\leq Q_{w,i}^{n}(0)+A_{i}^{n}(t), hence tight by monotonicity. By finite-dimensional tightness and the modulus-of-continuity criterion (Billingsley, 1999, Theorem 13.2), the full vector 𝒳¯n\bar{\mathcal{X}}^{n} is tight in 𝔻⁡([0,T],ℝd)\mathbb{D}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d}) under the J1J_{1} topology.

Continuity of limits.

By Prohorov’s theorem, extract a weakly convergent subsequence 𝒳¯nk⇒𝒳¯\bar{\mathcal{X}}^{n_{k}}\Rightarrow\bar{\mathcal{X}}. By the Skorokhod representation theorem, there exist versions of 𝒳¯nk\bar{\mathcal{X}}^{n_{k}} and 𝒳¯\bar{\mathcal{X}} defined on a common probability space such that 𝒳¯nk→𝒳¯\bar{\mathcal{X}}^{n_{k}}\to\bar{\mathcal{X}} almost surely in the J1J_{1} metric. Each coordinate of 𝒳¯n\bar{\mathcal{X}}^{n} has jumps of size ±1/n\pm 1/n. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the number of jumps exceeding ϵ\epsilon in 𝒳¯n\bar{\mathcal{X}}^{n} is zero for n>1/ϵn>1/\epsilon. Hence the limit 𝒳¯\bar{\mathcal{X}} has no jumps exceeding ϵ\epsilon for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, implying 𝒳¯\bar{\mathcal{X}} is almost surely continuous.

Identification of the limit.

For the arrival process, the FSLLN gives A¯in​(t)→λi​t\bar{A}_{i}^{n}(t)\to\lambda_{i}t uniformly on compacts. For time-changed processes, if Λ¯n​(t)→Λ​(t)\bar{\Lambda}^{n}(t)\to\Lambda(t) uniformly on compacts with Λ\Lambda continuous and strictly increasing, then N⁡(n​Λ¯n​(⋅))/n→Λ⁡(⋅)N(n\bar{\Lambda}^{n}(\cdot))/n\to\Lambda(\cdot) uniformly on compacts by the continuous mapping theorem and FSLLN. Since X¯in→xi\bar{X}_{i}^{n}\to x_{i} uniformly implies 1n​Λw,in​(t)=∫0tμw,i​X¯in​(s)​𝑑s→∫0tμw,i​xi​(s)​𝑑s\frac{1}{n}\Lambda_{w,i}^{n}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}\bar{X}_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds\to\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}x_{i}(s)\,ds, we obtain

D¯w,in​(t)→dw,i​(t)=∫0tμw,i​xi​(s)​𝑑s\bar{D}_{w,i}^{n}(t)\to d_{w,i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{w,i}\,x_{i}(s)\,ds

uniformly on compacts. The same argument applies to D¯j,in\bar{D}_{j,i}^{n}, D¯h,in\bar{D}_{h,i}^{n}, and B¯w,in\bar{B}_{w,i}^{n}. Taking limits in the flow-balance equations of the nn-system yields (26)–(27). The capacity constraints (28) hold since ∑iX¯in≤nw\sum_{i}\bar{X}_{i}^{n}\leq n_{w}, ∑iY¯in≤nj\sum_{i}\bar{Y}_{i}^{n}\leq n_{j}, ∑i(Z¯i,dn+Z¯i,jn)≤nh\sum_{i}(\bar{Z}_{i,d}^{n}+\bar{Z}_{i,j}^{n})\leq n_{h} for all nn, and weak inequalities are preserved under limits.

9.2 Proof of Lemma 4.1 (Single-Class Threshold Ordering)

Recall from (32):

nh(1)=μwμh​ppass​Jeff,nh(2)=μwμh​(nw−prej​Jeff),nh(3)=μwμh​nw.n_{h}^{(1)}=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}},\quad n_{h}^{(2)}=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\bigl(n_{w}-p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}\bigr),\quad n_{h}^{(3)}=\frac{\mu_{w}}{\mu_{h}}\,n_{w}.

Part (i): General ordering.

We prove nh(1)≤nh(2)≤nh(3)n_{h}^{(1)}\leq n_{h}^{(2)}\leq n_{h}^{(3)} without any condition on JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}}.

For the first inequality nh(1)≤nh(2)n_{h}^{(1)}\leq n_{h}^{(2)}, we need to show

ppass​Jeff≤nw−prej​Jeff.p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq n_{w}-p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}.

Rearranging,

ppassJeff+prejJeff≤nw⇔Jeff(ppass+prej)≤nw.p_{\mathrm{pass}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}+p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq n_{w}\quad\iff\quad J_{\mathrm{eff}}(p_{\mathrm{pass}}+p_{\mathrm{rej}})\leq n_{w}.

Since ppass+prej=1p_{\mathrm{pass}}+p_{\mathrm{rej}}=1 (a task routed through the judge is either passed or rejected), this simplifies to Jeff≤nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq n_{w}, which always holds because Jeff=min⁡{nw,J}≤nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}=\min\{n_{w},J\}\leq n_{w} by definition.

For the second inequality nh(2)≤nh(3)n_{h}^{(2)}\leq n_{h}^{(3)}, we need

nw−prejJeff≤nw⇔prejJeff≥0.n_{w}-p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq n_{w}\quad\iff\quad p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq 0.

Since prej≥0p_{\mathrm{rej}}\geq 0 and Jeff≥0J_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq 0, this always holds. Therefore, nh(1)≤nh(2)≤nh(3)n_{h}^{(1)}\leq n_{h}^{(2)}\leq n_{h}^{(3)} in general.

Part (ii): Strict ordering under non-degeneracy.

Now assume Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w}. From Part (i), Jeff​(ppass+prej)=Jeff≤nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}(p_{\mathrm{pass}}+p_{\mathrm{rej}})=J_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq n_{w}. Under Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w}, the inequality becomes strict, hence nh(1)<nh(2)n_{h}^{(1)}<n_{h}^{(2)}. For the second inequality, nh(2)<nh(3)n_{h}^{(2)}<n_{h}^{(3)} is equivalent to prej​Jeff>0p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}>0. Under the standing assumption qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha (equivalently β(I)+β(I​I)<1\beta^{(I)}+\beta^{(II)}<1, which requires α>0\alpha>0), we have prej≥α⁡(1−β(I​I))>0p_{\mathrm{rej}}\geq\alpha(1-\beta^{(II)})>0. Moreover, Jeff<nwJ_{\mathrm{eff}}<n_{w} with Jeff≥0J_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq 0; we note that Jeff=0J_{\mathrm{eff}}=0 is a degenerate case (no judge capacity) excluded by the four-phase analysis, so Jeff>0J_{\mathrm{eff}}>0. Therefore prej​Jeff>0p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J_{\mathrm{eff}}>0 and nh(2)<nh(3)n_{h}^{(2)}<n_{h}^{(3)}.

9.3 Proof of Proposition 4.3

Specializing the reduced multi-class LP to I=1I=1 yields the single-class 2D LP

maxx,v\displaystyle\max_{x,v}\quad x−β(I)​v\displaystyle x-\beta^{(I)}v (42a)
s.t. 0≤v≤x≤nw,\displaystyle 0\leq v\leq x\leq n_{w}, (42b)
v≤μjμw​nj,\displaystyle v\leq\frac{\mu_{j}}{\mu_{w}}\,n_{j}, (42c)
x−prej​v≤μhμw​nh,\displaystyle x-p_{\mathrm{rej}}v\leq\frac{\mu_{h}}{\mu_{w}}\,n_{h}, (42d)
x−β(I)​v≤λμw​(1−α).\displaystyle x-\beta^{(I)}v\leq\frac{\lambda}{\mu_{w}(1-\alpha)}. (42e)

Under the assumptions nw≥H+prej​Jn_{w}\geq H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}\,J and λμw​(1−α)≥nw\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{\mu_{w}(1-\alpha)}\geq n_{w}, we have x−β(I)​v≤x≤H+prej​J≤nw≤λμw​(1−α)x-\beta^{(I)}v\leq x\leq H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}J\leq n_{w}\leq\frac{\lambda}{\mu_{w}(1-\alpha)} for every feasible (x,v)(x,v) with binding human constraint, so both the worker constraint x≤nwx\leq n_{w} and the arrival constraint (42e) are slack. Dropping them, the LP (42) reduces to

maxx,v\displaystyle\max_{x,v}\quad x−β(I)​v\displaystyle x-\beta^{(I)}v
s.t. 0≤v≤x,v≤J,x−prej​v≤H.\displaystyle 0\leq v\leq x,\quad v\leq J,\quad x-p_{\mathrm{rej}}v\leq H.

Fix any v∈[0,J]v\in[0,J]. Since the objective is increasing in xx, the optimal choice of xx is the largest feasible one:

x⁡(v)=H+prej​v,x(v)=H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}v,

provided v≤x⁡(v)v\leq x(v), which is equivalent to ppass​v≤Hp_{\mathrm{pass}}v\leq H, i.e., v≤H/ppassv\leq H/p_{\mathrm{pass}} (well-defined since qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha implies ppass>0p_{\mathrm{pass}}>0).

Therefore the problem reduces to a one-dimensional maximization over 0≤v≤min⁡{J,Hppass}\displaystyle 0\leq v\leq\min\left\{J,\;\frac{H}{p_{\mathrm{pass}}}\right\} of

x⁡(v)−β(I)​v=H+(prej−β(I))​v.x(v)-\beta^{(I)}v=H+\bigl(p_{\mathrm{rej}}-\beta^{(I)}\bigr)v.

Using qacc=(1−α)​(1−β(I))ppass\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{(1-\alpha)(1-\beta^{(I)})}{p_{\mathrm{pass}}}, one checks the identity

prej−β(I)=ppass1−α​(qacc−(1−α)),p_{\mathrm{rej}}-\beta^{(I)}=\frac{p_{\mathrm{pass}}}{1-\alpha}\bigl(q_{\mathrm{acc}}-(1-\alpha)\bigr),

so the objective is (strictly) increasing in vv if qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha, (strictly) decreasing if qacc<1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}<1-\alpha, and constant in vv if qacc=1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}=1-\alpha.

Hence:

  • •

    If qacc>1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}>1-\alpha, the maximizer is v∗=min⁡{J,Hppass}\displaystyle v^{*}=\min\left\{J,\;\frac{H}{p_{\mathrm{pass}}}\right\}.

    • –

      If H≤ppass​JH\leq p_{\mathrm{pass}}J, then v∗=H/ppassv^{*}=H/p_{\mathrm{pass}} and x∗=H+prej​v∗=Hppass\displaystyle x^{*}=H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}v^{*}=\frac{H}{p_{\mathrm{pass}}}, hence ϕ∗=v∗x∗=1\displaystyle\phi^{*}=\frac{v^{*}}{x^{*}}=1.

    • –

      Otherwise v∗=Jv^{*}=J and x∗=H+prej​Jx^{*}=H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}J, hence ϕ∗=JH+prej​J\displaystyle\phi^{*}=\frac{J}{H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}J}.

  • •

    If qacc<1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}<1-\alpha, the maximizer is v∗=0v^{*}=0 and x∗=Hx^{*}=H, hence ϕ∗=0\phi^{*}=0.

  • •

    If qacc=1−αq_{\mathrm{acc}}=1-\alpha, every vv in the feasible interval attains the same objective value, and setting x∗=H+prej​v∗x^{*}=H+p_{\mathrm{rej}}v^{*} yields a (generically) non-singleton optimal set.

This proves Proposition 4.3.

Lemma 9.12 (Time-averaged constraints)
