x^in​(T)\displaystyle\hat{x}_{i}^{n}(T) :=1T​∫0TXin​(s)n​𝑑s,x^i,f​bn​(T):=1T​∫0TXi,f​bn​(s)n​𝑑s,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\frac{X_{i}^{n}(s)}{n}\,ds,\qquad\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n}(T):=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\frac{X_{i,fb}^{n}(s)}{n}\,ds,
v^in​(T)\displaystyle\hat{v}_{i}^{n}(T) :=1μw,i​T​Sw→j,in​(T)n,v^i,f​bn​(T):=1μw,i​T​Sw→j,i,f​bn​(T)n.\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\mu_{w,i}T}\,\frac{S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(T)}{n},\qquad\hat{v}_{i,fb}^{n}(T):=\frac{1}{\mu_{w,i}T}\,\frac{S_{w\to j,i,fb}^{n}(T)}{n}. (47)

Let x^i,+n​(T):=x^in​(T)+x^i,f​bn​(T)\hat{x}_{i,+}^{n}(T):=\hat{x}_{i}^{n}(T)+\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n}(T), v^i,+n​(T):=v^in​(T)+v^i,f​bn​(T)\hat{v}_{i,+}^{n}(T):=\hat{v}_{i}^{n}(T)+\hat{v}_{i,fb}^{n}(T), and

h^in​(T):=(x^in​(T)−prej,i​v^in​(T))+(x^i,f​bn​(T)−prej,i,f​b​v^i,f​bn​(T)).\hat{h}_{i}^{n}(T):=\big(\hat{x}_{i}^{n}(T)-p_{\mathrm{rej},i}\hat{v}_{i}^{n}(T)\big)+\big(\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n}(T)-p_{\mathrm{rej},i,fb}\hat{v}_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big).

Then, for any subsequential limit point as n→∞n\to\infty,

0≤vi≤xi,0≤vi,f​b≤xi,f​b.0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i},\qquad 0\leq v_{i,fb}\leq x_{i,fb}. (48)

Moreover, for all nn,

∑i∈ℐx^i,+n​(T)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\hat{x}_{i,+}^{n}(T) ≤nwnn,\displaystyle\leq\frac{n_{w}^{n}}{n}, (49a)
∑i∈ℐμw,iμj,i​v^i,+n​(T)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}\,\hat{v}_{i,+}^{n}(T) ≤njnn,\displaystyle\leq\frac{n_{j}^{n}}{n}, (49b)
∑i∈ℐμw,iμh,i​h^in​(T)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{h,i}}\,\hat{h}_{i}^{n}(T) ≤nhnn.\displaystyle\leq\frac{n_{h}^{n}}{n}. (49c)

Finally, defining

x^i,f​bn,gen​(T):=αi​(x^in​(T)−(1−βi(I​I))​v^in​(T)),\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n,\mathrm{gen}}(T):=\alpha_{i}\Big(\hat{x}_{i}^{n}(T)-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})\hat{v}_{i}^{n}(T)\Big), (50)

we have

0≤x^i,f​bn​(T)≤x^i,f​bn,gen​(T).0\leq\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\leq\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n,\mathrm{gen}}(T). (51)
Proof 9.13

proof: Fix ii. We have 0≤Sw→j,in​(T)≤Sw,in​(T)0\leq S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(T)\leq S_{w,i}^{n}(T) and the random time-change representation

Sw,in​(T)=Nw,i​(∫0Tμw,i​Xin​(s)​𝑑s),S_{w,i}^{n}(T)=N_{w,i}\!\left(\int_{0}^{T}\mu_{w,i}X_{i}^{n}(s)\,ds\right),

where Nw,iN_{w,i} is a unit-rate Poisson process. Hence,

0≤v^in​(T)≤1μw,i​T​Sw,in​(T)n=1T​∫0TXin​(s)n​𝑑s+o⁡(1)=x^in​(T)+o⁡(1),0\leq\hat{v}_{i}^{n}(T)\leq\frac{1}{\mu_{w,i}T}\frac{S_{w,i}^{n}(T)}{n}=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\frac{X_{i}^{n}(s)}{n}\,ds+o(1)=\hat{x}_{i}^{n}(T)+o(1),

and passing to a subsequential limit yields 0≤vi≤xi0\leq v_{i}\leq x_{i}. The feedback-type inequality 0≤vi,f​b≤xi,f​b0\leq v_{i,fb}\leq x_{i,fb} is identical. For all t≥0t\geq 0, the feedback network satisfies the pointwise capacity constraints

∑i∈ℐ(Xin​(t)+Xi,f​bn​(t))\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\big(X_{i}^{n}(t)+X_{i,fb}^{n}(t)\big) ≤nwn,\displaystyle\leq n_{w}^{n}, (52)
∑i∈ℐ(Yin​(t)+Yi,f​bn​(t))\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\big(Y_{i}^{n}(t)+Y_{i,fb}^{n}(t)\big) ≤njn,\displaystyle\leq n_{j}^{n},
∑i∈ℐ(Zin​(t)+Zi,f​bn​(t))\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\big(Z_{i}^{n}(t)+Z_{i,fb}^{n}(t)\big) ≤nhn,\displaystyle\leq n_{h}^{n},

We now derive (49a)–(49c) line by line. Integrating the worker constraint in (52) over [0,T][0,T], dividing by n​TnT, and using (47) gives

∑i∈ℐx^i,+n​(T)=1T​∫0T∑i∈ℐXin​(s)+Xi,f​bn​(s)n​𝑑s≤nwnn,\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\hat{x}_{i,+}^{n}(T)=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{X_{i}^{n}(s)+X_{i,fb}^{n}(s)}{n}\,ds\leq\frac{n_{w}^{n}}{n},

which is (49a). The judge and human constraints (49b)–(49c) follow by the same time-averaging argument applied to the second and third inequalities in (52) (with the normalizations chosen so that all constraints are written in AI-Worker service units, matching the LP).

To justify (51) without circularity, we compute the feedback-generation rate explicitly. Feedback tasks have no exogenous arrivals: they are created only when a fresh class-ii task is rejected by a human. In AI-Worker service units, fresh class-ii output is produced at rate μw,i​xi\mu_{w,i}x_{i}, of which a fraction vi/xiv_{i}/x_{i} is routed to the judge. Thus:

  • •

    Direct-to-human fresh flow: rate μw,i​(xi−vi)\mu_{w,i}(x_{i}-v_{i}). Each such task is rejected by a human with probability αi\alpha_{i}, generating feedback at rate μw,i​αi​(xi−vi)\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}(x_{i}-v_{i}).

  • •

    Judge-to-human fresh flow: among the judge-routed fresh flow (rate μw,i​vi\mu_{w,i}v_{i}), only judge-accepted tasks reach humans; conditional on judge acceptance, a human rejection occurs with probability αi​βi(I​I)/ppass,i\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{(II)}/p_{\mathrm{pass},i}, hence the feedback-generation rate contributed by this path equals

    μw,i​vi⋅ppass,i⋅αi​βi(I​I)ppass,i=μw,i​αi​βi(I​I)​vi.\mu_{w,i}v_{i}\cdot p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\cdot\frac{\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{(II)}}{p_{\mathrm{pass},i}}=\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{(II)}v_{i}.

Summing the two contributions gives the total feedback-generation rate (in tasks/time)

μw,i​αi​(xi−vi)+μw,i​αi​βi(I​I)​vi=μw,i​αi​(xi−(1−βi(I​I))​vi).\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}(x_{i}-v_{i})+\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{(II)}v_{i}=\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}\Big(x_{i}-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}\Big).

Dividing by μw,i\mu_{w,i} converts this to an AI-Worker service level upper bound, yielding the fluid balance inequality

xi,f​b≤αi​(xi−(1−βi(I​I))​vi),x_{i,fb}\leq\alpha_{i}\Big(x_{i}-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}\Big),

and the corresponding time-averaged generation term (50). Since feedback tasks may additionally be lost via worker-queue abandonment before entering AI-Worker service, the time-averaged feedback service level cannot exceed the time-averaged generation, which is exactly (51).

Lemma 9.14 (Relaxed LP and reward bound)

Fix T>0T>0. Let (xi,vi,xi,f​b,vi,f​b)(x_{i},v_{i},x_{i,fb},v_{i,fb}) be any subsequential limit point of (x^in​(T),v^in​(T),x^i,f​bn​(T),v^i,f​bn​(T))\big(\hat{x}_{i}^{n}(T),\hat{v}_{i}^{n}(T),\hat{x}_{i,fb}^{n}(T),\hat{v}_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big) as n→∞n\to\infty. Then (xi,vi,xi,f​b,vi,f​b)(x_{i},v_{i},x_{i,fb},v_{i,fb}) is feasible for the relaxed LP obtained from (39) by replacing the feedback flow-balance equality with the inequality

xi,f​b≤αi​(xi−(1−βi(I​I))​vi),i∈ℐ.x_{i,fb}\leq\alpha_{i}\big(x_{i}-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}\big),\qquad i\in\mathcal{I}. (53)

Moreover,

lim supn→∞1n​T​𝔼​[∑iri​(Cin​(T)+Ci,f​bn​(T))]≤∑iri​μw,i​[(1−αi)​(xi−βi(I)​vi)+(1−κi​αi)​(xi,f​b−βi(I)​vi,f​b)].\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i}r_{i}\big(C_{i}^{n}(T)+C_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big)\Big]\leq\sum_{i}r_{i}\,\mu_{w,i}\Big[(1-\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}\big)+(1-\kappa_{i}\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i,fb}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i,fb}\big)\Big]. (54)
Proof 9.15

proof: We establish feasibility and the reward bound in turn.

Feasibility. By Lemma 9.12, any subsequential limit point satisfies the box constraints (48), the time-averaged capacity constraints (49), and the feedback-generation inequality (51). Taking n→∞n\to\infty along the subsequence yields feasibility of (xi,vi,xi,f​b,vi,f​b)(x_{i},v_{i},x_{i,fb},v_{i,fb}) for the relaxed LP (53) together with the remaining constraints in (39).

Reward bound. Fix ii and TT. A human-accepted completion of a fresh task of class ii can occur only if the AI-Worker output is correct. Consider the two routing outcomes for each fresh worker completion:

  • •

    If it is routed directly to humans, then it can contribute at most one completion by time TT, and only if it is correct. Since each fresh worker completion is routed either to the judge or to the direct human path, the number routed directly to humans by time TT equals Sw,in​(T)−Sw→j,in​(T)S_{w,i}^{n}(T)-S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(T). Hence the expected number of such completions is bounded by (1−αi)​𝔼​[Sw,in​(T)−Sw→j,in​(T)](1-\alpha_{i})\,\mathbb{E}[S_{w,i}^{n}(T)-S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(T)].

  • •

    If it is routed to the judge, then it can contribute at most one completion by time TT, and only if it is correct and the judge does not falsely reject it. The probability of this event is (1−αi)​(1−βi(I))(1-\alpha_{i})(1-\beta_{i}^{(I)}). Hence the expected number of such completions is bounded by (1−αi)​(1−βi(I))​𝔼​[Sw→j,in​(T)](1-\alpha_{i})(1-\beta_{i}^{(I)})\,\mathbb{E}[S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(T)].

Adding the two bounds yields

𝔼⁡[Cin​(T)]≤(1−αi)​𝔼​[Sw,in​(T)]−(1−αi)​βi(I)​𝔼​[Sw→j,in​(T)].\mathbb{E}\big[C_{i}^{n}(T)\big]\leq(1-\alpha_{i})\,\mathbb{E}\big[S_{w,i}^{n}(T)\big]-(1-\alpha_{i})\beta_{i}^{(I)}\,\mathbb{E}\big[S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(T)\big].

Dividing by n​TnT and using the random time-change law of large numbers for Sw,in​(T)S_{w,i}^{n}(T) together with (47) yields

lim supn→∞1n​T​𝔼​[Cin​(T)]≤μw,i​(1−αi)​(xi−βi(I)​vi).\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}\big[C_{i}^{n}(T)\big]\leq\mu_{w,i}(1-\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}\big).

The same argument applies to feedback tasks, replacing the fresh error rate αi\alpha_{i} by the feedback error rate κi​αi\kappa_{i}\alpha_{i}, which yields

lim supn→∞1n​T​𝔼​[Ci,f​bn​(T)]≤μw,i​(1−κi​αi)​(xi,f​b−βi(I)​vi,f​b).\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}\big[C_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big]\leq\mu_{w,i}(1-\kappa_{i}\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i,fb}-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i,fb}\big).

Summing over ii and weighting by rir_{i} yields (54).

Lemma 9.16 (Relaxation is tight)

Let R~f​b∗\widetilde{R}_{fb}^{*} be the optimal value of the relaxed LP (i.e., (39) with (53) in place of the equality). Then R~f​b∗=Rf​b∗\widetilde{R}_{fb}^{*}=R_{fb}^{*}.

proof: Clearly R~f​b∗≥Rf​b∗\widetilde{R}_{fb}^{*}\geq R_{fb}^{*}. We show that every optimal solution of the relaxed LP satisfies the feedback flow-balance with equality, hence is feasible for the original LP.

The feedback inequality holds because ϵ<si/(1+αi)\epsilon<s_{i}/(1+\alpha_{i}) implies x~i,f​b=xi,f​b∗+ϵ≤αi​(x~i−(1−βi(I​I))​v~i)\tilde{x}_{i,fb}=x_{i,fb}^{*}+\epsilon\leq\alpha_{i}(\tilde{x}_{i}-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})\tilde{v}_{i}). The objective changes by ri​μw,i​[−(1−αi)+(1−κi​αi)]​ϵ=ri​μw,i​αi​(1−κi)​ϵ>0r_{i}\mu_{w,i}\bigl[-(1-\alpha_{i})+(1-\kappa_{i}\alpha_{i})\bigr]\epsilon=r_{i}\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}(1-\kappa_{i})\epsilon>0, contradicting optimality.

If βi(I)=1\beta_{i}^{(I)}=1, the same argument as Proposition 6.1 (Subcase 2b) applies. In all subcases, Δ>0\Delta>0, contradicting optimality.

Hence si=0s_{i}=0 for every ii, so R~f​b∗=Rf​b∗\widetilde{R}_{fb}^{*}=R_{fb}^{*}.

Upper bound.

By Lemma 9.14, for each fixed TT,

lim supn→∞1n​T​𝔼​[∑iri​(Cin​(T)+Ci,f​bn​(T))]≤Rf​b∗,\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i}r_{i}\big(C_{i}^{n}(T)+C_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big)\Big]\leq R_{fb}^{*},

and therefore

lim infT→∞lim infn→∞1n​T​𝔼​[∑iri​(Cin​(T)+Ci,f​bn​(T))]≤Rf​b∗.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\;\liminf_{n\to\infty}\;\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i}r_{i}\big(C_{i}^{n}(T)+C_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big)\Big]\leq R_{fb}^{*}. (55)
Lemma 9.18 (Fluid convergence under feedback Fluid-Tracking)

Let (xi​(⋅),xi,f​b​(⋅))(x_{i}(\cdot),x_{i,fb}(\cdot)) be any feedback fluid limit under 𝛑n,f​b\bm{\pi}^{n,fb}. Then, for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I},

xi​(t)→xi∗,xi,f​b​(t)→xi,f​b∗,vi​(t)→vi∗,vi,f​b​(t)→vi,f​b∗.x_{i}(t)\to x_{i}^{*},\qquad x_{i,fb}(t)\to x_{i,fb}^{*},\qquad v_{i}(t)\to v_{i}^{*},\qquad v_{i,fb}(t)\to v_{i,fb}^{*}. (56)
Proof 9.19

proof: Fix ii. Under 𝛑n,f​b\bm{\pi}^{n,fb}, each fresh class-ii worker completion is routed to the judge with probability ϕi∗:=vi∗/xi∗\phi_{i}^{*}:=v_{i}^{*}/x_{i}^{*} (and to the direct human path otherwise), and each feedback class-ii worker completion is routed to the judge with probability ϕi,f​b∗:=vi,f​b∗/xi,f​b∗\phi_{i,fb}^{*}:=v_{i,fb}^{*}/x_{i,fb}^{*} (with the convention 0/0:=00/0:=0). Equivalently, there exist i.i.d. Bernoulli routing indicators {ξi,k}k≥1\{\xi_{i,k}\}_{k\geq 1} with ℙ⁡(ξi,k=1)=ϕi∗\mathbb{P}(\xi_{i,k}=1)=\phi_{i}^{*} and {ξi,f​b,k}k≥1\{\xi_{i,fb,k}\}_{k\geq 1} with ℙ⁡(ξi,f​b,k=1)=ϕi,f​b∗\mathbb{P}(\xi_{i,fb,k}=1)=\phi_{i,fb}^{*} such that, for all t≥0t\geq 0,

Sw→j,in​(t)=∑k=1Sw,in​(t)ξi,k,Sw→j,i,f​bn​(t)=∑k=1Sw,i,f​bn​(t)ξi,f​b,k.S_{w\to j,i}^{n}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{S_{w,i}^{n}(t)}\xi_{i,k},\qquad S_{w\to j,i,fb}^{n}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{S_{w,i,fb}^{n}(t)}\xi_{i,fb,k}.

By the strong law of large numbers for Bernoulli thinnings (applied to these random sums) and the fluid scaling, along any fluid-limit subsequence we have

vi​(t)=ϕi∗​xi​(t),vi,f​b​(t)=ϕi,f​b∗​xi,f​b​(t),for a.e. ​t≥0.v_{i}(t)=\phi_{i}^{*}x_{i}(t),\qquad v_{i,fb}(t)=\phi_{i,fb}^{*}x_{i,fb}(t),\qquad\text{for a.e.\ }t\geq 0.

Let xi+​(t):=xi​(t)+xi,f​b​(t)x_{i}^{+}(t):=x_{i}(t)+x_{i,fb}(t) and xi+,∗:=xi∗+xi,f​b∗x_{i}^{+,*}:=x_{i}^{*}+x_{i,fb}^{*}. If xi+​(t)>xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)>x_{i}^{+,*}, admissions are blocked and x˙i+​(t)=−μw,i​xi+​(t)<0\dot{x}_{i}^{+}(t)=-\mu_{w,i}x_{i}^{+}(t)<0. If xi+​(t)<xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)<x_{i}^{+,*} and the class-ii worker queue is nonempty, admissions occur and x˙i+​(t)>0\dot{x}_{i}^{+}(t)>0. Hence xi+​(t)→xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)\to x_{i}^{+,*}. To make the drift statement explicit, note that in any feedback fluid limit xi+​(⋅)x_{i}^{+}(\cdot) satisfies a.e.

x˙i+​(t)=ui+​(t)−μw,i​xi+​(t),\dot{x}_{i}^{+}(t)=u_{i}^{+}(t)-\mu_{w,i}x_{i}^{+}(t),

where ui+​(t)u_{i}^{+}(t) is the (fluid) admission rate of class-ii jobs into AI-Worker service (fresh plus feedback). Under the admission rule, ui+​(t)=0u_{i}^{+}(t)=0 whenever xi+​(t)≥xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)\geq x_{i}^{+,*}, which yields x˙i+​(t)=−μw,i​xi+​(t)\dot{x}_{i}^{+}(t)=-\mu_{w,i}x_{i}^{+}(t) on {xi+(t)>xi+,∗}\{x_{i}^{+}(t)>x_{i}^{+,*}\}. When xi+​(t)<xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)<x_{i}^{+,*} and the worker queue for class ii is positive, the policy admits class-ii jobs whenever worker capacity becomes available, implying ui+​(t)>μw,i​xi+​(t)u_{i}^{+}(t)>\mu_{w,i}x_{i}^{+}(t) and hence x˙i+​(t)>0\dot{x}_{i}^{+}(t)>0. This yields a one-dimensional monotonicity/Lyapunov drift argument for |xi+​(t)−xi+,∗||x_{i}^{+}(t)-x_{i}^{+,*}| and implies xi+​(t)→xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)\to x_{i}^{+,*}.

Let qw,i,f​b​(t)q_{w,i,fb}(t) be the feedback worker-queue fluid mass. By Theorem 3.1 applied to the feedback state vector (the proof uses only the Poisson/exponential primitives and random time-change representations, hence extends verbatim to the duplicated feedback network), any fluid limit satisfies the corresponding mean-rate flow equations; in particular the feedback arrival rate equals the fresh human-rejection rate μw,i​αi​(xi​(t)−(1−βi(I​I))​vi​(t))\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}\big(x_{i}(t)-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}(t)\big) and the abandonment rate is θi​qw,i,f​b​(t)\theta_{i}q_{w,i,fb}(t). Hence the feedback-queue dynamics satisfy

q˙w,i,f​b​(t)=μw,i​αi​(xi​(t)−(1−βi(I​I))​vi​(t))−μw,i​xi,f​b​(t)−θi​qw,i,f​b​(t)\dot{q}_{w,i,fb}(t)=\mu_{w,i}\alpha_{i}\big(x_{i}(t)-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}(t)\big)-\mu_{w,i}x_{i,fb}(t)-\theta_{i}q_{w,i,fb}(t)

whenever qw,i,f​b​(t)>0q_{w,i,fb}(t)>0. Under admission priority to feedback tasks, the equilibrium satisfies qw,i,f​b∗=0q_{w,i,fb}^{*}=0 and xi,f​b∗=αi​(xi∗−(1−βi(I​I))​vi∗)x_{i,fb}^{*}=\alpha_{i}(x_{i}^{*}-(1-\beta_{i}^{(II)})v_{i}^{*}). Together with xi+​(t)→xi+,∗x_{i}^{+}(t)\to x_{i}^{+,*}, this yields xi,f​b​(t)→xi,f​b∗x_{i,fb}(t)\to x_{i,fb}^{*} and xi​(t)→xi∗x_{i}(t)\to x_{i}^{*}, and thus vi​(t)→vi∗v_{i}(t)\to v_{i}^{*} and vi,f​b​(t)→vi,f​b∗v_{i,fb}(t)\to v_{i,fb}^{*}.

Lower bound.

By Lemma 9.18, the feedback fluid reward rate converges to Rf​b∗R_{fb}^{*}, i.e.,

∑iri​μw,i​[(1−αi)​(xi​(t)−βi(I)​vi​(t))+(1−κi​αi)​(xi,f​b​(t)−βi(I)​vi,f​b​(t))]→Rf​b∗.\sum_{i}r_{i}\,\mu_{w,i}\Big[(1-\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i}(t)-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i}(t)\big)+(1-\kappa_{i}\alpha_{i})\big(x_{i,fb}(t)-\beta_{i}^{(I)}v_{i,fb}(t)\big)\Big]\to R_{fb}^{*}.

Applying Theorem 3.1 to the enlarged feedback state vector is valid: the feedback model preserves the same Poisson/exponential primitives and random time-change representations, with all f​bfb-type processes being duplicates of the baseline ones, and the endogenous feedback generation being an internal flow count. Moreover, the routing rule is implemented by i.i.d. thinnings with fixed probabilities (ϕi∗,ϕi,f​b∗)(\phi_{i}^{*},\phi_{i,fb}^{*}), which is compatible with the fluid-scaling law of large numbers. Using standard long-run averaging (Dai, 1995),

lim infT→∞lim infn→∞1n​T​𝔼𝝅n,f​b​[∑iri​(Cin​(T)+Ci,f​bn​(T))]≥Rf​b∗.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\;\liminf_{n\to\infty}\;\frac{1}{nT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\bm{\pi}^{n,fb}}\Big[\sum_{i}r_{i}\big(C_{i}^{n}(T)+C_{i,fb}^{n}(T)\big)\Big]\geq R_{fb}^{*}. (57)

Combining (55) and (57) proves the theorem.

Since β(I)=1\beta^{(I)}=1, the fresh objective contribution is (1−α)​(x−β(I)​v)=(1−α)​(x−v)=0(1-\alpha)(x-\beta^{(I)}v)=(1-\alpha)(x-v)=0 at any point with v=xv=x, so the objective change comes entirely from the feedback term (1−κ​α)​(xf​b−β(I)​vf​b)(1-\kappa\alpha)(x_{fb}-\beta^{(I)}v_{fb}). Because v~f​b=vf​b∗\tilde{v}_{fb}=v_{fb}^{*}, the change is

Δ=μw​(1−κ​α)​[(x~f​b−β(I)​v~f​b)−(xf​b∗−β(I)​vf​b∗)]=μw​(1−κ​α)​A​δ=μw​(1−κ​α)​α​β(I​I)​δ>0.\Delta=\mu_{w}(1-\kappa\alpha)\bigl[(\tilde{x}_{fb}-\beta^{(I)}\tilde{v}_{fb})-(x_{fb}^{*}-\beta^{(I)}v_{fb}^{*})\bigr]=\mu_{w}(1-\kappa\alpha)\,A\delta=\mu_{w}(1-\kappa\alpha)\alpha\beta^{(II)}\delta>0.

This contradicts optimality.

In both cases, the assumption s>0s>0 leads to a contradiction. Therefore s∗=0s^{*}=0, which yields qw,f​b∗=0q_{w,fb}^{*}=0 and the flow balance xf​b∗=α⁡(x∗−(1−β(I​I))​v∗)x_{fb}^{*}=\alpha(x^{*}-(1-\beta^{(II)})v^{*}) stated in LP (37).

9.10 Proof of Proposition 6.4 (Worker-Judge Coupling)

Proof 9.22

proof: Let (nw,nj,{xi,vi})(n_{w},n_{j},\{x_{i},v_{i}\}) be any optimal solution for (41) at which the human constraint binds. Since the objective depends only on (xi,vi)(x_{i},v_{i}) and not directly on (nw,nj)(n_{w},n_{j}), we may modify the capacities while keeping (xi,vi)(x_{i},v_{i}) fixed, provided feasibility is preserved.

Define the used worker and judge capacities by

n^w:=∑ixi,n^j:=∑iμw,iμj,i​vi.\widehat{n}_{w}:=\sum_{i}x_{i},\qquad\widehat{n}_{j}:=\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}\,v_{i}.

Because (nw,nj,{xi,vi})(n_{w},n_{j},\{x_{i},v_{i}\}) is feasible, we have n^w≤nw\widehat{n}_{w}\leq n_{w} and n^j≤nj\widehat{n}_{j}\leq n_{j}. Hence

γw​n^w+γj​n^j≤γw​nw+γj​nj≤B,\gamma_{w}\widehat{n}_{w}+\gamma_{j}\widehat{n}_{j}\leq\gamma_{w}n_{w}+\gamma_{j}n_{j}\leq B,

so (n^w,n^j,{xi,vi})(\widehat{n}_{w},\widehat{n}_{j},\{x_{i},v_{i}\}) is also feasible for (41). It attains the same objective value, since (xi,vi)(x_{i},v_{i}) is unchanged. By construction, the worker and judge constraints are both binding at this new optimal solution:

∑ixi=n^w,∑iμw,iμj,i​vi=n^j.\sum_{i}x_{i}=\widehat{n}_{w},\qquad\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}\,v_{i}=\widehat{n}_{j}.

Now suppose moreover that the budget is slack at the original optimal solution, i.e.,

γw​nw+γj​nj<B.\gamma_{w}n_{w}+\gamma_{j}n_{j}<B.

Choose any ϵw,ϵj>0\epsilon_{w},\epsilon_{j}>0 small enough that

γw​(n^w+ϵw)+γj​(n^j+ϵj)≤B.\gamma_{w}(\widehat{n}_{w}+\epsilon_{w})+\gamma_{j}(\widehat{n}_{j}+\epsilon_{j})\leq B.

Then (n^w+ϵw,n^j+ϵj,{xi,vi})(\widehat{n}_{w}+\epsilon_{w},\widehat{n}_{j}+\epsilon_{j},\{x_{i},v_{i}\}) is feasible and has the same objective value as before, while now both capacity constraints are strict:

∑ixi=n^w<n^w+ϵw,∑iμw,iμj,i​vi=n^j<n^j+ϵj.\sum_{i}x_{i}=\widehat{n}_{w}<\widehat{n}_{w}+\epsilon_{w},\qquad\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{w,i}}{\mu_{j,i}}\,v_{i}=\widehat{n}_{j}<\widehat{n}_{j}+\epsilon_{j}.

Thus there exists an optimal solution in which both the worker and judge constraints are slack.

Therefore, if the human constraint binds, there exists an optimal solution in which the worker and judge constraints are either both binding or both slack.
